24.
General.
The rules promulgated by the Supremne Court of the United States as of
date of March 7, 5921t, governing pro eedlngs in admiralty, shall apply and be
in force in all admiralty proceedings ini this court.
a5,
Verification.
Pleadings in rem or in personam, claims and answers to interrogatories,
except on behalf of the United States, shall be verified by the oath or affirmation
of the party, or in his absence, by his agent, attorney in fact, or proctor. It
such verification be made by the agent, attorney in fact, or proctor, it shall
state the source of his knowledge or information; declare that the document
verified is true to the best of his knowledge, Information, and belief, and the
reason why the verification is not made by the party,
26,
Amendments.
Amendments, or supplementary matters, must be connected with the libel
or other pleadings by appropriate reference, without recapitulation or restate,
rent of the pleading amended or added to,

27.
Security for Costs.
No libel, petition, or answer shall be filed, except on the part of the United
iAt s, and in suits for seamen's wages, and suits in forma pauperis, unless the
Ph offering the same shall first file a bond or stipulation for costs, with two
ore sufficient sureties, one of whom shall reside or maintain a place of busi
ness within the Canal Zone, conditioned that the principal shall pay all costs
awarded against him by this court, and, lu case of appeal, by the appellate court.
In suits in personam, sucht bond or stipulation shall be in the sum of $;oo;
in suits in rem, or where process of foreign attacliireint is to be issued, the bond
or stipulation shall be in the sum of $250.
Salvors coming into port in possession o& the propcvty libeled, petitioners
for money in the Registry of the Court, and The Panama Canal, shall not be
required to give such security,
'Bonds and S ti pulstiratsa.
Unless otherwise ordered and approved by the Court, all bonds and stipuw
lations for costs, for the discharge of property arrested, for stay of eascutioni
of any process in rem, or in any other case wherein a bond or stipulation Is
required of the party appearing in the sit, under the satute or the admiralty
or equity rules of the court, Shall be executed and delivered by the party with
two or more sufficient sureties, one of whom shall be a resident or maintain an
office and place of business within the Canal zone, conditioned, to answer the
final decree of the Court, whether such decree shall be rendered in the original
or the appellate court,
tn lieu of sureties, the party may file his stipulation condition ed as above
set forth, accompanied by the deposit of cash, or the manager's cheek of a solvent
bank, or United States bonds ini the amount or sunt required, the same to bedelivered to the Marshal, or deposited in the R4egistry of the Court, as the
exigency of the case may demand, and such cash, manager's check, or United

States bonds shall be subject to all money demands of parties to the suit, as may
be determined by the final decree of the court; Provided, the bond of any
responsible surety company in w *if United States, and acceptable to the Court,
may be taken in lieu of the security and surety above mentioned, on the condition
that the bond so given and taken shall waive all questions as to the jurisdiction
of the court to enter judgment in any proceedings wherein said bond shall
have been given,

29.
Return Day of Process,
Original process on libels and information shall be made returnable on the
first Monday of each month at a stated or special term; provided, that twenty
running days have elapsed since the last. publication of a monition or the service
of process; and in cases where such delay of twenty days shall not have expired
on the first Monday of the month, said process shall be returnable on the third
Monday of the same month,
Upon process in remt, the return shall state the day of seizure or of sale, as
the case me Pr be.

30.
Release of Property on Bond.
The Marshal shall stay execution of any warrant of arrest or other process
in rem, or discharge the property arrested, upon receiving from the claimant a
bond or stipulation for double theta mount claimed by libellant, with sufficient
surety, approved by the judge, or, in hiis absence, by the Marshal, conditioned
to answer the decree of the Court in the cause, as provided in Section 941 of
the United States Revised Statutes, as amended by the Act of Congress approved
March 3, 189o (30 Statutes, 1354), The bond so taken shall run in favor of the
Marshal for the benefit of all parties in interest, and shall be immediately deliv-
ered by the Marshal to the Clerk of the court, who shall file the same in the
record.
But the parties to the suit may, by written agreement filed in the cause,
consent that the stipulation shall be reduced to such an amount as they may deem
sufficient to secure the claim of the libellant and intervenors and costs, without
in any manner impairing its validity.
In salvage cases the amount of the release bond shall be fixed by the Court
or by agreement between the proctors for the libellant and claimant.
3',
Amount to be Stated.
In all suits, except for salvage, the amount claimed by the libellant or
intervenors must be specifically stated in their pleadings.
32,
Clerk to Issue Process.
The Clerk or Assistant Clerk of the court is authorized to issue all admiralty
and other process without any special order, except in cases where the statute
or the admiralty or equity rules require an order of the Court, or of the judge,
to authorize process. He may also issue all writs of dedimus potestatent and
commissions to take depositions of absent witnesses, as authorized by the Act
of Congress approved March 9, '892, but shall issue letters rogatory only when
ordered by the Court.

33.
Mesne Process.
Mesne process may be either in personain or in rein or both.
Process in personanm may be:

clauses.label: (i)
clauses.text:
(i) A simple citation in the nature of a summons to appear and
answer to the suit.
6

j 14

(2) Such a citation, with a clause therein that if the respondent
cannot be found, his goods and chattels to the amount sued for be
attached,

(3) Such a citation and attachment, together with a clause of
foreign attachment of the respondent's property and credits to the
amount sued for in the hands of garnishees named therein.
The names of the garnishees and the specific property in their
hands, if known, shall be stated in the libel or petition and in the
process, and the garnishees shall be cited to appear and answer on oath.

(4) A warrant of arrest of the person shll issue only upon the
special order of the Court~ alone, or with an attachment,
In suits in personam, except on a libel for liquidated damages not
exceeding $500, no process of attachment or foreign attachment shall
issue, unless allowed by special order of the Court, upon due proof of
the demand and of the propriety of the attachment being first made.
Process in rem shall be:

clauses.label: (i)
clauses.text:
(i) By a warrant to arrest the ship, goods, or other things to be
arrested, with a monition to all persons interested therein, and shall
be issued as, of course, by the Clerk of the court upon the filing of the
libel and security for costs.

34.
Division of Docket Fee and Costs.
In cases for salvage, when several parties are entitled to participate therein,
the docket fee and costs taxable by statute in favor of the prevailing party shall
be divided equally among the proctors of the respective parties who share in
the salvage.

35.
ibels-When to Stand as Interventions,
When property is already under seizure by process of this court, all libels
filed against the same property shall stand and be considered as interventions
in the original case, and but one proctor's fee shall be allowed, which shall go
to the proctor in the original cause. The Clerk shall be authorized to make all
orders permitting interventions to be filed in all proceedings in rem.

36.
Payment Into Court,
In all actions for sums certain, the claimant or respondent may pay into
court the amount claimed in the libel, with accrued interest and costs, and may
thereupon have an order entered, instanter, for the restoration of his property.
37,
Stipulations on Intervening Libels,
Any third person who shall intervene in any cause of admiralty, and mari-time jurisdiction in rem shall be required to give a stipulation, with surety in
the sum of $25, to abide by the final (decree rendered in the cause, and pay all
such costs, expenses and damages as shall be awarded by the Court upon final
decree, whether it is rendered in the original or appellate court, and such inter-
venor shall also deposit the sum of Sio with the Clerk to secure his costs.

38.
Deposits for Costs.
Neither the Clerk nor the Marshal shall be required to issue or serve any
process, or to perform any service for parties, until their costs and the necessary
expenses incident to the service shall be paid or secured to their satisfaction,
except in cases of seanmen', wages and suits in fornma pauperis.

15

39.
Publication of Process,
Upon any seizure in suits in rem, or upon any information in rem or in
personam wherein publication is required by law, such notice shall be published
once unless the Court by special order, directs other or further publication.
Publication hereunder, unless otherwise ordered, shall be at least one week
before the date on which the process is made returnable. The published notice
need contain only the title of the suit, the nature of the cause of action, the
amount demanded, the time and place of the return of monition and the names
of the Marshal and proctor, and shall direct all persons interested to appear or
that default and condemnation will be ordered.

40.
Publication Notice of Sale.
Public notice of the sale of property after condemnation in suits ini rem,
shall be made by publication in a newspaper of general circulation within the
Canal Zone, for at least six successive days, unless otherwise ordered in the
decree, t «: last; publication thereof to be at least fifteen days before the date of
said sale, as provided in U, S. Revised Statutes, section 939. (U, S. Comp.
Statl, 1918, Sec. xg65,)
4'.
Testimony to be taken before a Commissioner.
In all cases of admiralty and maritime jurisdiction the evidence of witnesses
present at the place where the court is held shall be taken orally before a Corn-
missioner, upon at least cue day's notice to the opposite party; provided, that
either side may set the caso for trial in open court on the question of liability,
in which event all witnesses within the jurisdiction will be heard orally. The
stenographer employed shall W~ entitled to receive twenty-five cents per hundred
words as compensation for his services, and shall furnish one copy of the evidence
to the proctor for the opposite party, without charge, when requested.

42.
Evidence by Written Interrogatories,
Evidence taken under dedimnus potestateml, or under commission as pro-
vided in the Act of Congress approved March 9, 182, shall be by written inter-
rogatories propounded to the witness, filed in the Clerk's office, and a certified
copy of the same shall be served on the opposite party, together with a notice
by the Clerk that he is required to file cross-interrogatories, if any he has, within
five days from a date to be specified in such notice.
In case the opposite party is absent from the Canal Zone and not repre-sented by an attorney, service on the interrogatories and notice to cross may be
made by posting the same at the court house for the period of five days.
At the expiration of the time so allowed the Clerk, or Assistant Clerk, shall
issue the proper writ or commission.

43.
Time for Taking Evidence.
After issue joined, the libellant shall have sixty days in which to take his
evidence, and thereafter the claimant or respondent shall have the like time to
take his evidence, and no more, unless for cause shown the Court shall enlarge
or restrict the time, and provided the case is not heard in open court.
44"
Notice to Set Cause for Trial,
After the expiration of the time for taking evidence has expired, either
party may set the cause down for trial on motion upon five days' notice, served

16
on the adverse party or his proctor; but, in case the adverse party be absent
and not represented, the notice may be served by posting the cause for trial at
the court house for the period of five days.

45.
Certificate of Counsel, and Affidavit to Exceptions, etc.
Every exception or plea to at libel or intervening libel shall be accompanied
by a certificate of counsel that, in hit opinion, it is well funded in law, and be
supported by affidavit of the party or his proctor that it is not interposed for
delay, aind that the facts stated therein ate true to the best of his knowledge,
infor matron and belief.
46,
Intervening Libels,
No intervening libel setting up a claiui either or in addition to the amount
claimed in the original libel, whereby the liability of the surety on the release
bond would be increased, shall be allowed in any case after the property seized
has been released.
47,
Trial on Libel and Answer.
The libellant shall have the right, upon the coming in of the answer, to set
the cause down for trial on the libel and answer in all cases where the facts are
substantially admtitted, and nothing remains but que~stionx of law for decision.
In such cases the avermnents of the answer, well pleaded, except avermnents of
law, shall, for the purpose of the trial, be taken as true.

48.
Interventions in Remn.
Iuttrventionas filed in proceedings in rem shall be considered as denied, and
neted not be answered, but parties whose interts are itltolved mtay, at theft
option, plead, answer or demur thereto.

49.
Third Patty Practice.
If a defendant shall, by petition on oath, filed before answer, or within
such further time as the Court may allow, allege fault in any other party, in
respect of the matters complained of in the libel, or shall allege that he is entitled
to contribution or indemnity from any other party in respect of such matters,
and shall pray that such other party be brought into the suit as a party defendatt
in analogy with the provisions of Admiralty Rule 57 of the Supreme Court of
the United States, process on such petition may be issued and the cause shall
proceed otherwise as 'in cases under the 57th Rule.

30.
Note of Evidence-Testimony to be Bound, etc.
Before the final hearing each party shall file with the Clerk a written list
of the testimony and proofs on which fie wishes to be heard, with all such testi-mnony and proofs, and no testimony and proofs not so listed and filed shall be
considered by the Court or be included in the record on appeal. The testimony
shall be boud, consecutively paged, and indexed. No ease shall be set down
for argument or final hearing until this Rule has been complied with.

53.
Objections to Evidence.
Nor bectiou to the admissbiity of evidence taken wnder Rule 41 shall he
scored mart spoled at the time the evidence is taken, nor shall any ob ee-

17
tions to interrogatories propounded to witnesses examined under commission
be considered unless made by the opposite party at the time cross-interrogatories
are filed or before the commission issued; and parties making objection or
objections to the manner and form in which a commission has been executed
shall do so by motion to suppress.

52.
Confirmation of Commissioners' Reports.
Exceptions to Commissioners' Reports shall be filed within twenty days
after the date of the filing of the Report. Should no exceptions or opposition
be filed within said delay, the report may be confirmed on motion of counsel.

53.
Matters Not Specifically Provided For.
In any matter not provided for in the general admiralty rules of the Supreme
Court of the United States or in these rules, the rules of practice in admiralty
in the United States District Courts of the Southern District of New York shall
be made applicable and apply in this court.

The Alien Property Custodian is hereby authorized to sell at private sale,

able, without public or other advertisement, certain real estate now being held
and administered by him as such Alien Property Custodian and heretofore,

property of MARIE BROCKM LLE R, of Germany, which said person he did after
investigation determine to be an enemy within the purview of said Act as
amended, which real es~jate is described as follows, to-wit:-
A one-half interest, subject to any dower right claimed by Fidelia G.
Harpenau, in and to Lot 38, in the Borough of Brooklyn, City of New York,
County of Kings, State of New York, at the Southwest corner of 86th treet
and Bay 25th Street; a frontage on 86th Street of 96 feet 8 inches and a front-
age on Bay 25th Street of too feet, known on Tax Map as Section 19, Block
6375, Lot 38;
And Lot 43 in the Borough of Brooklyn, City of New York, County of
Kings, State of New York, situate on the west side of Bay 25th Street 120
feet south of 86th Street; having a frontage of 120 feet on Bay 25th Street
and a depth on either side of 96 feet 8 inches known on Tax Map as Section
19, Block 6375, Lot 43; together with improvements thereon.
My reasons for the foregoing determination, order, rule and regulation
are:

clauses.label: (a)
clauses.text:
(a) Non-enemies own the other undivided one-half interest in said real
estate and are desirous of sale for distribution of the proceeds among the
parties entitled thereto, and have agreed to accept for their respective interests
their proportionate part of the sale price of FORTY-Six THOUSAND DOLLARS
($46,oo) .

clauses.label: (b)
clauses.text:
(b) Said property is encumbered by dower rights belonging to a non-enemy
who has agreed to commute the same and consents to said sale at said price.

clauses.label: (c)
clauses.text:
(c) The price of FORTY Six THOUSAND DOLLARS ($46,ooo) for the entire
property appears to be adequate and is probably more than could be obtained
at public auction.

clauses.label: (d)
clauses.text:
(d) To sell the property by proceedings in Court for the purpose of dis-
tribution of proceeds would entail more expense and probably produce a smaller
price than to accept the offer of FORTY Six THOUSAND DOLLARS ($46,0), one-
half of which is to be paid for the enemy interest in said real estate. In addi-
tion the proposed method will relieve the trust of said unnecessary expense,
also of delay and inconvenience, which should be avoided.

clauses.text:
589. Scope of Duties-It is the duty of consular officers to -protect and
promote the national economic interests of the United States. To this end they
are required-
(I) To endeavor to create, each in. his own district, a situation favorable
to the importation and sale of American goods (general measures of trade
promotion);

(3) To reply to the private inquiries of American citizens touching com-
mercial and industrial matters; and

(4) To lend aid and advice to American citizens having or contemplating
business in their several districts.
The emphasis in trade promotion should be upon the development of the
export trade of the United States; but the mutuality of trade interests and the
benefits flowing from a well-balanced commercial exchange, make it also desir-
able that American merchants and manufacturers be assisted in purchasing
abroad raw materials and goods which are not in direct competition with the
products of American industry.
59o. Study of distric.-A consular officer should confine his commercial
activities, and especially his trade reporting, to matters pertaining to his district.
As prerequisite to the proper fulfillment of his commercial functions, he will
familiarize himself, as soon as possible after arrival at his post, with the main
facts constituting the economic life of his district. The manner in which inf.'-
mation is obtained must necessarily vary, but none of the following methods
may properly be omitted:
(I) Study of the more important reports of the officer's predecessor, espe-
cially those covering the last year.

(2) Perusal of other available published reports, monographs and books of
a dependable character containing information concerning the country or
district.

(3) Examination of statistical and other reports, pertaining to the country
or district, published currently by the local government.

clauses.label: (a)
clauses.text: (a) Regular reading of the better newspapers and trade journals.

(5) Personal contact with leading local business men and officials.
~A.
'+:: h f " -I- ran r..F.

2
GENERAL MEASURES OF TRADE PROMOTION.

591. Enforcement of treaty and other rights.-The United States has treaties
with many countries securing within their territories to American citizens
general liberty of commerce and navigation. Consular officers in a country
with which there is such a treaty should study carefully its provisions, and watch
over their observance by the local government. Even where no treaty exists,
they should be vigilant to detect acts detrimental to the interests of American
trade, and of a kind to be considered inconsistent with international commercial
comity. Consular officers are empowered by treaty in the case of some coun-
tries, and in general they are conceded the right by usage, to make complaint
to the local authorities concerning the infraction of treaties, and for the purpose
of protecting the rights and interests of their countrymen. When consular
officers feel they have reason to believe that treaty rights of American citizens
have been infringed, a report should be promptly submitted to the Department
of State and to the supervising consul general, if there be one, or to the American
diplomatic representative. Consular officers will also submit to the supervising
consul general, or to the diplomatic representative, if there be no consul general,
and to the Department of State any general information or observations they
may have to impart touching the rights and interests of American commerce
under treaty and usage.

592. Removal of obstacles to free importation of American goods.-Local laws
and administrative regulations should have the careful attention of consular offi-
cers, more particularly those having to do with the tariff, the customs and port
administrations, warehousing and transportation, quarantine and the sanitary
control of food stuffs. They should also study ocean and inland freight rates,
and other conditions of transport. When it is thought that there is discrimina-
tion against American goods in respect to any of these matters, or that modifica-
tions in the substance, or manner of application of such regulations or rates,
would stimulate the sale of American goods, and the desired modiAfications can
not readily be obtained by application to the local authorities, a full report,
with explicit recommendations as to the modifications considered desirable,
should be made to the supervising consul general, if there be one, or to the
diplomatic representative, if there be no consul general, and to the Department
of State.

593. Creation of demand for American goods.-In addition to facilitating
the importation and sale of American goods in their respective districts, as
indicated in the foregoing paragraphs, consular officers should endeavor to
create and foster an active demand for them on the part of local merchants.
The acquaintance of importers should be carefully cultivated, and the high
order of merit which in the main attaches to all classes of exports from the
United States should be impressed upon them whenever fitting opportunity
offers. The consulate should be made known to the local business community
as a center to which it may resort for information of all kinds respecting
American goods. Statistical and other publications relating to American
trade should be placed at the disposal of all serious inquirers. In particular,
directories of American manufacturers should be displayed for convenient
reference, and every facility afforded in connection with their use.

594. American chambers of commerce abroad.-American chambers of com-
merce, or similar organizations, have been formed in a number of the more
important commercial centers abroad by American citizens and others having
an interest in American business. As these organizations are normally impor-
tant and helpful factors in the development of trade between the United States
and foreign countries, consular officers should lend them hearty support and
cooperation in all their proper activities. In places where such organizations

3
do not already exist and the-number of American residents and the importance
of American business seem sufficient to support them, consular officers should,
within the limitations mentioned below, take an active part, or even assume
the initiative, in any movement for their creation, provided that the projectcdi
organization, by its serious, dependable and truly American character, com-
mends itself to their judgment as being likely to subserve the development of
American trade and the national interests of the United States. In cities where
it is impracticable to organize active chambers of commerce, the formation of
various types of American societies or clubs may be encouraged with a view to
helpful exchanges of opinion and common action in matters of special interest
to the American community.
Officers are cautioned to avoid lending support to unworthy enterprises
and to avoid in any case becoming so closely identified with any chamber of
commerce, or similar organization, that they may be considered by the local
public, or firms or persons in the United States, as sponsors for the business
reliability and financial integrity of the members of the organization.. For this
reason consular officers are not permitted to accept active offices in chambers
of commerce, or similar organizations, but they may, and in appropriate circum-
stances should, act in honorary or advisory capacities. The law forbids the use
of any public funds for the payment of membership dues in any society or
association, unless authorized by specific appropriation.-37 Stat. L. 184.
Consular -fficers while in the United States may not solicit memberships
for chambers of commerce in their districts, or contributions thereto, but may
inform interested persons of the facts relating to the establishment, organiza-
tion, and operation of these organizations, conditions of membership, dues,
etc. They should refer any who may consider application for membership to
the secretary or other appropriate officer of the organization with whom they
may correspond.
COMMERCIAL REPORTS AND REPORTING.

595. Object and general character.-The main object in view in the prepara-
tion of commercial reports should be to supply accurate information for the
use of the Government and the American business community in a general
expansion of American trade.
Such reports should present a faithful reflex of +he actual conditions of
which they treat. Consuls should not yield to any temptation to construe
facts or figures in advocacy of their individual theories and opinions. They
should not, on the other hand, be mere transmitters of objective data. In
addition to setting forth plainly and impartially statistics and positive infor-
mation, the reporting officer should furnish, in distinct paragraphs, an analyt-
ical interpretation of the material presented, and, when appropriate, a full
statement of his personal deductions and opinions.
Data must be obtained, as far as possible, from official sources, and the
origin must in all cases be clearly indicated. When quotations are given, they
should be carefully designated as such with the proper quotation marks, in
order that they may not be confused with individual views or conclusions by
the writer. In those portions of reports which are intended for publication,
reference should be omitted to political or controversial matters, and particular
care should be exercised to avoid unfavorable comments or criticism upon the
government, people, or institutions of the country of the consul's residence.
It is a part of a consul's duty to transmit promptly to the Department of
State commercial information of a political or controversial nature whenever it
appears that the interests of the United States, or of American commerce, may
be subserved thereby; but such communications should be in the form of sepa-rate despatches or special sections of reports conspicuously marked "Confiden-
tial ", intended for the information of the Government alone.

4

596. Reports to be submitted only to Department of State.-The statutes on
the subject-R. S. Sec. 1712; 32 Stat. L. 827.--contemplate that the Depart-
ment of State shall be the sole medium through which consular reports shall
reach other governmental departments or the public. Consular officers are
accordingly prohibited from furnishing copies of their reports, or articles upon
the trade or commerce of their districts, to any publication, to private persons,
or directly to other departments. Such reports will be transmitted only to the
Department of State, and the fact that they have been prepared should not be
disclosed without special permission until after they have been published.

597. Annual report.-Every consular officer in charge of a consular office
is required to submit to the. Secretary of State, as soon as possible after the close
of each calendar year, a report on the development of commerce and industries
in his district during the year in question. This Annual Report should present
a concise summary of the economic progress or retrogression during the year ini
question of the country or consular district under consideration. It should be
prepared at the earliest possible moment after the annual trade statistics of the
country or district are available. Consular officers should acquaint themselves
with the sources of these statistics and should endeavor to obtain advance.
copies whenever practicable. The statistical tables published by the foreign
governments should be sent as enclosures with the Annual Report, and only the
important statistical tables and summaries need be reproduced in the report
itself. The tables used in the Annual Report should give the figures for the
year under review and the preceding year only, but it is also desirable to set
forth figures for total imports and exports covering a series of years.
The Annual Report should be confined largely to comment upon the out-
standing features of the year's trade and should dwell upon industrial conditions
and development only in brief form and in case they affect American trade in
some important degree.
597a. Periodical Reports.-In order that the Department may be kept fully
informed throughout the year upon all economic developments that may be of
interest to the American business public concise periodical reports upon the
commerce and industries of each consular district are required. They should
contain a general picture of the developments which have taken place within
the district during the period under review. These reports will be used for the
information of the Department of State, and by the Bureau of Foreign and
Domestic Commerce in the preparation of its periodical reviews of various
countries and geographical units.

598. Annual declared export return.-Within twenty days after the close of
each calendar year a return shall be submitted in duplicate to the Department
of State, on Form No. 20, of the exports declared for shipment to the United
States and its dependencies during the year in question at the consular office
and the agencies subordinate to it, if any. This return is in the nature of a
commercial report, and is not to be included in the accounts and returns but
forwarded separately. The return shall include the following separate state-
ments or tables: (i) Itemized quantities and values of exports to the United
States; (2) same for Porto Rico; (3) same for Hawaii; (4) same for the Philip-
pine Islands; and (5) itemized quantities and values of returned American goods,
if any. When there have been no exports to any one or more of the dependen-
cies mentioned, the fact should be specifically stated on the return. Returns
of exports declared at consular agencies should be separate from, but should
be prepared in the same manner as the returns from principal officers.

599. Special reports.-From time to time the Secretary of State addresses
to consular officers circular or particular instructions calling for reports on
special subjects. In complying with these instructions officers should in every
instance endeavor to be prompt in reply, and accurate in statement. Whenever

5
it seems likely that the gathering of the necessary data will involve delay, theDepartment should be advised at once of the reasons therefor, and the date atwhich the report will probably be forwarded.
6oo. Voluntary reports.-Consular officers are expected to report on theirown initiative concerning all matters arising in their districts of a kind tointerest or be of use to the American business community or to the Governmentin its efforts to protect and promote American trade. In respect to manysubjects it will not suffice to report accomplished facts, but officers shouldstudy the probable course of development in that they may foresee, and pointit out in time to be of use.
6oi. Trade opportunities.-Consular officers should be especially watchfuland alert to discern and to report promptly all concrete opportunities whichmay arise within their districts for the extension of American trade or thefurtherance of American commercial, industrial, and financial interests.6oa. List of foreign firms.-There shall be maintained in each consularoffice a list or file, in the form prescribed by the Secretary of State, of the prin-cipal commercial and industrial firms in the consular district. Copies of thislist shall be furnished to the Secretary of State as he shall direct. Brief speciallists of foreign firms interested in specific classes of business shall also be pre-pared, as directed in Paragraph 6o-c.
REPLIES TO TRADE INQUIRIES.
6o3. Trade inquiries to be answered promptly and specifically.-Inquiries oncommercial subjects received from American citizens, or those acting in theinterest of American trade, should be answered promptly, specifically, and fullywithin the limitations stated in the two succeeding paragraphs. The interestof the inquirer in the development of export trade is usually serious, and adecision whether to enter particular fields may rest upon the replies receivedfrom consular officers. There is need, therefore, for carefully considered, per-
tinent and comprehensive information. In cases where a complete answercan not be given at once, prompt acknowledgment should be made, to be fol-lowed later by a more detailed reply.
6o3a. Limitations on replies to trade inquiries-Consular officers may notcorrespond with private persons as to the political affairs of foreign governments(Paragraph 436.) They must not comment unfavorably upon the institutionsor acts of the Government of the country in which they are assigned, nor givepublicity to opinions or statements of :act which reflect unfavorably on thecustoms and manners of the people.
Requests by private persons or firms for information of any kind relatingto the business of competing Americani firms should be refused. In describingmarket conditions to inquirers care should be exercised to avoid mention byname of other American products or of American firms competing in the same
market.
Consular officers should, in no circumstances, disclose information aboutAmerican firms or their business to other American firms, whether or not theyare competitors in the same line of goods. However, this should i'n no wiseprevent officers from giving full information concerning foreign markets, namesof importers, rates of duties, and specific suggestions for the extension of traderelations. Consular officers should discreetly reply to requests for information
about other American firms to the effect that such information should be pro-cured from the appropriate American manufacturer or head office in the United
States.
The records of American citizens registered at consulates, and records ofinvoices certified, are confidential, and must not be used as sources of informa-tion in replying to inquiries.

6
Consular officers should refuse requests for expression of opinion as to the
value of trade publications of all kinds, and as to the merits of particular articles
which are sold under trademarks or are patented. Replies to these requests
should be of such a character as to preclude their being used for or construed
as testimonials.
6o3b. Use of name as reference; financial standing of foreign firms.--Consular
officers are forbidden to vouch for the financial standing and for the general
responsibility of business men or enterprises. They may, however, refer such
inquirers to banks or other business agencies, and in replying should, whenever
practicable, discreetly give information regarding the general reputation of the
firms or individuals as to whom inquiry has been made, the number of years
they have been established, the general character and volume of their business,
and other facts of the same nature, such as may be readily ascertained.
6o3c. Special lists of foreign firms.-Special lists of foreign firms interested
in specific lines of trade should be prepared for use in connection with replies to
trade inquiries. When necessary a list should be prepared especially to meet
the exact needs of the inquirer. Lists may be arranged, in the discretion of the
consular officer, in the order either of the importance and reputability of the
firms listed, or of their probable usefulness to the inquirer.
6o3d. Waiver of responsibility.-Every list of foreign persons or firms which
is furnished to an inquirer by a consular officer with a view to the establishment
of business relations must be headed by an express waiver of responsibility,
stating that the consular officer can accept no responsibility in any way for the
persons and firms named, and suggesting means by which the inquirer may
inform himself in this respect, such as banks, business organizations, or reporting
agencies.
6o3e. Information sheets to accompany trade letters.-In order to shorten
the replies to trade inquiries and facilitate the investigations of the inquirers,
consular officers are directed to prepare, and transmit with each trade letter an
information sheet, setting forth the main facts of commercial importance
respecting their districts.
6o3f. To be transmitted through Department.-All consular correspondence
touching matters of trade in any way whatsoever must be forwarded to the
addressees through the Department of State, unless otherwise specifically
authorized by the Department.
OTHER DIRECT SERVICES.
603g. Aid and advice to citizens visiting district.-Consular officers will give
all proper aid and advice to American citizens visiting their districts on com-
mercial and other business, and to the traveling salesmen and other representa-
tives abroad of American manufacturers and exporters. They should endeavor
to facilitate in every proper way the legitimate business in connection with
American trade interests which these persons have in hand, not only by furnish-
ing them with needful information, but by aiding them to establish relations
with business firms and officials with whom it is necessary or desirable that they
become acquainted. At the same time they will carefully avoid the appear-
ance of lending official endorsement to the enterprises in which these persons
are interested.
6o3h. Not to act as agent.-Consular officers are forbidden by law to assume
in any way the role of business agent for particular concerns. They must not
solicit orders for them, nor undertake the distribution of samples or printed
matter, although catalogues, and, when the facilities of the office permit, small
samples may properly be received for display in the consulate, and the names
of particular firms may be supplied in response to appropriate inquiries. They
must not execute purchasing commissions of importance for private firms or
individuals except at the direction of the Department of State.

7
6o3i. Prosecution of private claims; collection of debts.-It is no part of the
duty of consular officers to attend to the collection of commercial debts or to
the prosecution of other private claims of American citizens in foreign counries,
although in appropriate cases they should use their good offices to effect amicable
adjustments, and in general they should have such relationships in the busi-
ness communities of their districts as will enable them to mediate successfully
in bringing about an amicable adjustment. When mediation has, however,
proved unsuccessful, or when the consul apprehends that his interference would
be inexpedient, or might be detrimental to the standing and dignity of the
consulate, he should limit his action to furnishing the names of reputable per-
sons competent to act for the inquirer in the premises, such as lawyers, banks,
or collection agencies.
6o3j. Complaints against American exporters.-When complaints are made
against American exporters by their foreign customers, in apparent good faith,
consular officers should endeavor to effect a satisfactory adjustment, with a
view to protecting the national commercial reputation of the United States.
They may, within their discretion, write directly to the American parties in
interest, transmitting the letter as usual through the Department of State.
Such letters should include a full statement of the facts ascertainable, together
with copies of all pertinent correspondence and documents. They should take
the form of a request for information or explanation, and carefully avoid an
assumption of dereliction on the part of the addressees. When it is felt that the
difficulty can not be handled in this manner, the consular officer will transmit
the data concerning the trade dispute under a covering despatch, enclosing a
separate memorandum setting forth in detail the allegations of the complainant
together with any evidence furnished in Siupport thereof. The covering despatch
should furnish the consular officer's views and deductions with regard to the
subject matter of the complaint. The memorandum should contain the facts
of the case in such form as to permit its submission to the American firm con-
cerned. Both the covering despatch and the memorandum should be for-
warded to the Department in triplicate.
603k. Surveys.-Consular officers are sometimes asked to appoint boards of
survey to examine and report on the condition of American merchandise im-
ported into foreign countries of which complaint has been made by the im-
porters. A consul has no statutory authority in this respect, and the findings
of such a board would be without conclusive effect in the United States.
Nevertheless, if the local law does not forbid, consuls should accede to requests
of this character, using their best efforts and judgment to find impartial experts
competent to the work in hand. The findings of the board may be forwarded
by the Consul, through the Department of State, to the exporter in the United
States, together with any comments he may consider appropriate. Oaths of
the surveyors to their findings are unnecessary, but may be administered when
requested by the party calling for the survey, a fee of $2.00 (item 33 of the
tariff of fees) being charged.
603-1. Trade conferences.-When consular officers visit thc United States
personal conferences may be arranged, in appropriate circumstances, between
them and American manufacturers and exporters, in order that the latter may
learn by direct interchange, of the opportunities for the establishment or exten-
sion of their trade in the officer's district. Consular officers may at the same
time learn from American manufacturers and exporters the viewpoint o~ the
American seller, his facilities for handling foreign trade, and his requirements
and expectations. Consular officers are required, before leaving their posts for
the United States, to prepare themselves especially for these interviews; and,
upon their return from the United States, or immediately before their departure
therefrom, to submit to the Department of State a detailed report of con-
ferences held.

8
COOPERATION IN TRADE PROMOTION.
6o3m. As the success of trade promotion work depends to a great extent
upon coordination of effort, the fullest cooperation is required between consuls,
supervising consuls general, and the diplomatic missions; and the cooperative
spirit shown by individual consular officers in adjusting their efforts to the
demands of national or regional coordination will be considered in determining
their efficiency ratings in trade promotion.
As an important part of their functions supervising consuls general are
charged with the general direction of trade promotion activities in their respec-
tive jurisdictions, and are authorized, subject to the approval of the Department
of State, to issue to the consuls resident therein instructions designed to obviate
duplication of effort, and to give harmony to their commercial activities.
Supervising consuls general should not, however, exercise their authority
in such a manner as unduly to discourage initiative or voluntary effort on the
part of the consuls in their jurisdictions. The special knowledge, judgment,
and interest possessed by each principal consular officer with~ regard to his
district must be recognized, and, so far as may be consistent with the avoidance
of duplication and unnecessary effort, each such officer must be given unlimited
opportunity for the preparation of reports on all matters arising in his district
and primary responsibility for the protection and promotion of American trade
therein.
Commercial attaches, as members of the diplomatic missions, like other
members thereof, have no formal relations with consular officers except
through the chiefs of mission. Such correspondence as a chief of mission may
authorize a commercial attache to conduct in his own name with consular
officers must pass through the supervising consul general.

(b) The term "qualified aircraft observer", as used in these regulations,
shall be construed to include any commissioned or warrant officer or enlisted
man of any branch of his respective service who has been, or may hereafter be
rated an Airplane Observer or Balloon Observer by competent authority in the
Army, or who has been, or may hereafter be appointed a Naval Aviation
Observer by competent authority in the Navy or Marine Corps, or who has
been, or may hereafter be appointed a Coast Guard Aviation Observer by
competent authority in the Coast Guard.

clauses.label: (c)

(c) The term "student aviator", as used in these regulations, shall be
construed to include any officer or warrant officer in any branch of his respective
service who is appointed a Student Naval Aviator by competent authority in
the Navy or Marine Corps, or who is. appointed a Student Coast Guard Aviator
by competent authority in the Coast Guard, and who is duly assigned to a
course of instruction in piloting aircraft.

clauses.label: (d)

(d) The term " student aviation pilot", as used in these regulations, shall
be construed to include any enlisted man in any branch of his respective serv-
ice who is appointed a Student Naval Aviation Pilot by competent authority
in the Navy or Marine Corps, or who is appointed a Student Coast Guard
Aviation Pilot by competent authority in the Coast Guard, and who is duly
assigned to a course of instruction in aircraft pilot duties.

clauses.label: (e)
clauses.text:

shall be construed to include any officer, warrant officer, or enlisted man, in
any branch of his respective service, who is appointed a Student Naval Aviation
Observer by competent authority in the Navy or Marine Corps, or who is
appointed a Student Coast Guard Aviation Observer by competent authority
in tihe Coast Guard, and who is duly assigned to a course of instruction in air-
craft observer duties.

2. Each officer or warrant officer who is a qualified aircraft pilot and who
is not unfit for duties as such, and whno is commissioned in, or duly assigned or
attached to tihe Air Service of the Army, or who is duly assigned to duty in any

Serve for the Army, the Chief of Bureau of Navigation for the'Ta~vy, e
Major General Cmadn o h Marine Carp, orv the Captain Coi-
mandant for the CoastGuard, and such detail shall remain in fore for tie entire
period of such commission, assignment, or attachment, except as hereinafter
provided in paragraphs 9 and to.

3. Each officer or warrant officer who is a qualified aircraft observer, or
an aircraft pilot who is unfit for piloting duties but is fit and desired for other
flying duty, and who is commissioned in, or duly assigned, or attached to the
Air Service of the Army, or who is duly assigned to duty in any part of the
aeronautic organization of the Navy, Marine Corps, or Coast Guard, shall be
detailed to duty involving flying; such detail shall be made by the Chief of
Air Service for the Army, the Chief of Bureau of Navigation for the Navy,
the Major General Commandant for the Marine Corps, or by the Captain Com-
mandant for the Coast Guard, and such detail shall remain in force for the
entire period of such commission, assignment, or attachment except as herein-
after provided in paragraphs 9 and to.
.. Each officer of the Medical Corps of the Army, or the Navy who is
duly assigned to duty with any aeronautic headquarters or unit of the Army,
Navy, Marine Corps, or Coast Guard, or assigned to duty at a station where
there is an aeronautic unit, and who has qualified as a flight surgeon, shall be
considered as on duty involving flying when detailed to such duty involving
flying by the Chief of Air Service for the Army, or by the Chief of Bureau of
Navigation for the Navy and Marine Corps, and such detail shall remain in
force for the entire period of such assignment, except as hereinafter provided
in paragraphs 9 and to.

5. Each officer or warrant officer other than student aviators of the Navy,
Marine Corps, and Coast Guard, and those specified in paragraphs 2, 3, and 4,
who is duly assigned to duty that includes flights in aircraft, shall be detailed
to duty involving flying; such detail shall be made by the Chief of Air Service
for the Air Service of the Army, the Secretary of War for other branches of
the Arms', the Chief of Bureau of Navigation for the Navy, the Major General
Commandant for the Marine Corps, or by the Captain Commandant for the
Coast Guard, and such detail shall remain in force for the entire period of such
assignment, except as hereinafter provided in paragraphs 9 and to.

6. Each officer, warrant officer or enlisted man of the Army who is duly
assigned to a course of instruction for qualification as aircraft pilot or aircraf t
observer, and each officer, warrant officer or enlisted man of the Navy, Marine
Corps or Coast Guard who is duly appointed a student aviator, a student avi-
ation pilot, or a student aviation observer, shall be detailed to duty involving
flying; such detail shall be made by the Chief of Air Service for the Army, the
Chief of Bureau of Navigation for the Navy, the Major General Commandant
for the Marine Corps, or by the Captain Commandant for the Coast Guard,
and such detail shall remain in force for the entire period of his course of in-
struction except as hereinafter provided in paragraphs 9 and to.

7. Each enlisted man who is serving in the Air Service of the Army, or in
any part of the aeronautic organization of the Navy, Marine Corps, or Coast
Guard, and who is a qualified aircraft pilot, shall be detailed to duty involving
flying by his commanding officer; such detail shall remain in force for the entire
period of such service, except as hereinafter provided in paragraphs 9 and To or
until revoked by his commanding officer; such detail and its revocation shall be
reported to the Chief of Air Service for the Army, the Chief of Bureau of Naviga-
tion for the Navy, the Major General Commandant for the Marine Corps, or to
the Captain Commandant for the Coast Guard.

8. Each enlisted man who is serving in the Air Service of the Army, or in
any part of the aeronautic organization of the Navy, Marine Corps, or Coast
Guard, and who is not a qualified aircraft pilot or observer, but is assigned to
duty that includes flights in aircraft, shall be detailed to duty involving flying
by his commanding officer; such detail shall remain in force for the entire period
of such assignment except as hereinafter provided in paragraphs 9 and to, or
until revoked by his commanding officer; such detail and its revocation shall
be reported to the Chief of Air Service for the Air Service of the Army, the

3
Secretary of War for other branches of the Army, the Chief of Bureau of Navi-
gation for the Navy, the Major General Commandant for the Marine Corps, or
to the Captain Commandant for, the Coast Guard.

9. Each officer, warrant officer or enlisted man of the Army, Navy, Marine
Corps, or Coast Guard, who is detailed to duty involving flying, shall be required
to make at least ten flights or be in the air a total of four hours during each
calendar month; provided that an officer, warrant officer, or enlisted man so
detailed, who is unable to meet these requirements' during any calendar month
for any reason other than sickness or injury, shall be regarded as having met
them if he performs a minimum of twenty flights or is in the air a minimum of
eight hours prior to the end of the following calendar month ; provided further,
that an officer, warrant officer or enlisted man so detailed, who is unable to meet
this alternative requirement for any reason other than sickness or injury, shall
be regarded as having met this requirement if he performs a minimum of thirty
flights or is in the air a minimum of twelve hours prior to the end of the calendar
month thereto succeeding. Failure to comply with the foregoing requirements
shall have the effect of suspending the detail to duty involving flying, but only
for the period during which the foregoing requirements as to flights are not
complied with; provided that, in the case of any officer, warrant officer, or en-
listed man, who, by reason of sickness or injury incurred in the line of duty, is
unable to comply with the foregoing requirements, his detail to duty involving
flying shall be considered as temporarily suspended from the day following that
on which the disability occurred; if the flight requirements are subsequently
met within the three months' period herein prescribed, the temporary suspen-
sion shall be considered nullified, otherwise it shall remain in effect until he
resumes flights in conformity with the foregoing requirements. Each officer,
warrant officer or enlisted man, who is detailed to duty involving flying, and
who is a qualified aircraft pilot, and who is fit for duty as such, shall make the
flights herein required as pilot. Each officer, warrant officer, or enlisted man who
is detailed to duty involving flying and who is a qualified aircraft observer, but is
not a qualified aircraft pilot, shall make the flights herein required as observer.

10. A commanding officer shall suspend from flying any officer, warrant
officer, or enlisted man under his command, who, in his opinion, is unfit for
flying for any reason other than sickness or injury. Such action shall be re-
ported, with the reasons therefor, for confirmation to the authority who issued
to such officer, warrant officer, or enlisted man his detail to duty involving
flying. The confirmation of such action shall have the effect of suspending the
detail to duty involving flying of the officer, warrant officer, or enlisted man
concerned from the date such suspension from flying was made. When any
officer, warrant officer or enlisted man, so suspended from flying, becomes in
the opinion of his commanding officer, again fit for flying, the commanding
officer shall revoke his suspension from flying and such action shall be reported,
with reasons therefor, for confirmation to the authority who confirmed the sus-

Executive Orber
Under authority of the Act of Congress approved June 30, 1882 (22 Stat. L.,
12 n), which prescribes that the Army and Navy General Hospital at Hot Sprins
7Arkansas, "shall be subject to such rules, regulations, and restrictions as shall
4 '~ be provided by the President of the United States," the following amendments,
effective July i, 1922, are hereby made to the rules and regulations prescribed
for the government of the said hospital by Executive Order of August 25, 1892,
as amended by later orders, viz:
i. This hospital shall be devoted to the treatment of the personnel indicated
below:

clauses.label: (a)
clauses.text:
(a) Beneficiaries of the United States Veterans' Bureau entitled to hospitali-
zation, except women, upon the requests of the proper representatives thereof.

clauses.label: (b)
clauses.text:
(b) Officers, commissioned warrant officers, warrant officers, ad enlisted
men of the Armmy, the Navy, and the Marine Corps, on the active lists, Army
Field Clerks (male), Field Clerks Quartermaster Corps, (male), and cadets at the
Military Academy and midshipmen at the Naval Academy, subject to such
rules as may be prescribed by the Wa and Navy Departments respectively.

clauses.label: (c)
clauses.text:
(c) Officers and enlisted men of the Coast Guard, and officers of the Public
Health Service, on the active lists, and cadets and cadet engineers of the Coast
Guard, under such rules as may be prescribed by the Treasury Department; and
officers and enlisted mnen of the Coast and Geodetic Survey, on the active lists,
tinder such rules as may be prescribed by the Department of Commerce.

clauses.label: (d)
clauses.text:
(d) Officers, commissioned warrant officers, warrant officers, pay clerks, and
enlisted men of the Army, the Navy, the Marine Corps, the Coast Guard, and
the Coast and Geodetic Survey, and officers of the Public Health Service, on the
retired lists or the equivalent thereof, under such rules as may be prescribed by
the Secretary of War

clauses.label: (e)
clauses.text:
(e) Honorably discharged officers, commissioned warrant officers, warrant
officers, Army Field Clerks (male), Field Clerks Quartermaster Corps (male),
cadets, cadet engineers and enlisted men of the Army, the Navy, the Marine
Corps (including National Guard Forces, Naval Militia, volunteers and drafted
or selected men in the service of the United States), tie Coast Guard and the
Coast and Geodetic Survey, and honorably discharged officers of the Public
Health Service, under such conditions and regulations as may be prescribed by
the Secretar 'of War.,.t"rr.
() When practicable, and for a reasonable time, under such conditions as
may be prescribed by the Secretary of War, male civilians employed by the
United States in H-ot Springs and its vicinity who sustain personal injuries
while in the performance of duty.

2. The rations of enlisted men of the Army on the active list while under
treatment in the hospital will be commuted at the rate of 6o cents a ration to be
paid to the commanding officer of the hospital by the post finance officer or such
other officer as may be designated, conformably to the regulations governing
the subsistence of enlisted patients at other Army hospitals.

3. Since there is no issuing quartermaster at this post, and rations in kind
can not in any~ case be economically issued, the rations of the enlisted men of the
Army on duty at this hospital will be commuted at the rate of 6o cents a ration,
to be paid to the men by the finance officer upon their individual receipts, con-
formable to tile regulations governing such payments in other Army cases.

4. The subsistence of enlisted men of the Navy, Marine Corps, Coast Guard,
and Coast and Geodetic Survey, on the active lists, under treatment in this
hospital in pursuance of orders, will be paid for to the commanding officer of the
hospital 
at the rate of 6o cents a day by the proper officers of the Navy Depart-Flo

ment, Coast Guard, and Coast and Geodetic Survey, upon monthly statements
of amounts due certified by the commanding officer of the hospital direct to the
Surgeon General of the Navy, the Captain Commandant of the Coast Guard,
and the Director of the Coast and Geodetic Survey, respectively.
S. The subsistence of members of the Nurse Corps on duty in this hospital
will be paid for by them monthly to the commanding officer of the hospital at
the rate of 6o cents a day.

6. Subsistence charges will be collected from other pay patients as follows:
Enlisted men of the Army, Navy, Marine Corps, Coast Guard, and Coast and
Geodetic Survey, on the retired lists, and honorably discharged officers, commis-
sioned warrant officers, warrant officers, Army Field Clerks, Field Clerks Quar-
termaster Corps, cadets, midshipmen, cadet engineers, and enlisted men of the
Army, the Navy, the Marine Corps (including National Guard forces, Naval
Militia, volunteers, and drafted or selected men, in the service of the United
States), the Coast Guard, and the Coast and Geodetic Survey, and honorably
discharged officers of the Public Health Service, subsisted on the status of en-
listed men, at 8,9 cents a day.
Military and naval cadets, midshipmen, and cadets and cadet engineers of
the Coast Guard, at 8o cents a day.
Officers, commissioned warrant officers, warrant officers, Army Field
Clerks, Field Clerks Quartermaster Corps, and Pay Clerks, of the Army, Navy,
Marine Corps, Coast Guard, Coast and Geodetic Survey, and Public Health
Service, and honorably discharged officers, commissioned warrant officers, war-
rant officers, Army Field Clerks, Field Clerks Quartermaster Corps, cadets, mid-
shipmen, cadet engineers, and enlisted men, of the Army, Navy, Marine Corps,
Coast Guard, Coast and Geodetic Survey and Public Health Service, subsisted
on the status of officers, at not exceeding $1.5o a day.

7. Medicine charges will be collected at 25 cents a day from pay patients as
follows :
Honorably discharged officers, commissioned warrant officers, warrant offi-
cers, Army Field Clerks, Field Clerks Quartermaster Corps, cadets, midshipmen,
cadet engineers and enlisted men of the Army, Navy, Marine Corps, Coast
Guard, Coast and Geodetic Survey, and Public Health Service.

8. In the cases of patients admitted upon account of the United States
Veterans' Bureau, subsistence charges at 85 cents a day will be billed and
submitted with W. D. Form No. 351 properly accomplished, by the commanding
officer of the hospital direct to the local finance officer for settlement by check.
Other expenses of Veterans' Bureau patients will be adjusted between the
appropriations concerned in conformity with orders issued by the Secretary of
War from time to time.

9. In the cases of patients admitted upon account of the United States
Employees' Compensation Commission, subsistence charges at 8,9 cents a day
for those on the status of enlisted men, and at not exceeding $ .50o a day for
those on the status of officers, and medicine charges at 25 cents a day for those
in either status, will be billed by the commanding officer direct to the Com-
mission. No other charges will be billed or collected in these cases.
io. Collections arising from subsistence charges will be taken up and
accounted for as hospital funds. Collections arising from medicine charges
will be turned over, on War Department Form No. 322a, to the nearest dis-
bursing or agent officer for deposit with the Treasurer of the United States to
the credit of the proper appropriations, which will be designated on W. D.
Form No. 322a, and accounted for in due form accordingly.
WARREN G HARDING
