clauses.text:
18. Consular fees.-Whenever any master or commander of a vessel of the
United States has occasion for any consular or other official service which any
consular officer of the United States s l lb authorized by la,' or usage officially
to perform, he shall apply to the consular officer at the consulate where such
service is required, to perform such service ; but no vessel's fees shall be
collected by consular officers from such a vessel. (Paragraph 52)-R. S., sec.
718; 23 Stat. L. 56. Sec. 12. The masters of vessels which are wholly owned
by citizens of the United States, and which are not registered, or enrolled and
licensed, shall pay to the consular officer the fees prescribed in the Tariff of
United States Consular Fees for such service.-iS Op. Att. Gen., 234.,,E-
Paragraph 103 is amended to read as follows: 7 ,~,.

193. Seamen ma~y be hired in forein por.-Every' master of a vessel in the
foreign trade may engage any seaman at any port out of the United States, in
the manner provided by law, to serve for one or more round trips from and to
the port of departure, or for a definite time, whatever the destination; and the
master of a vessel clearing from a port of the United States with one or more
seamen so engaged in a foreign p)ort is not required to reship such seamen in a
port of the United States, nor, upon the vesse's return to the United States, is
he liable to a penalty for failure to produce such seamen. And the master of a
vessel in the foreign trade may engage a seaman at any port in the United
States, in the manner provided by law, to serve on a voyage to any port, or for
the round trip from and to tihe port of departure, or for a definite time, what-
ever the destination. So, too, the master of a vessel making regular and stated
trips between the United States and a foreign country may en gage a seaman
for one or more round trips, or for a definite time, or on the return of said vessel
to the United States may reship such seaman for another voyage in the same
vessel, in the manner provided by law, without the payment of additional
fees to any officer for such reshipment or reengagement. It will thus be seen
that a master has full power to ship his crew, or any part of it, "by the run",
or for a given port or time, or for a round trip, and such shipments may be
made either in foreign or domestic ports.-23 Stat. L. 58, Secs. 19 and 20.
(Paragraph 205.)
Paragraph 195 is amended by inserting tile word " undocumented" before
the word " American " in the first line of the paragraph.
Paragraph 196 is amended to read as follows:

196. Additions to shipping articles:-Consular officers will be careful to
enter the shipment of seamen oil the original articles until the space is ex-
hausted; and whenever it becomes necessary to use additional articles, they
should firmly attach them to the original articles in such a manner that the new
articles can not be separated from the original without discovery or mutilation.
Paragraph 197 is amended to read as follows:

197. New art icles.-When it is necessary to grant new articles to a vessel,
the crew of which was named in articles given at a port of tile United States, the
consular officer shall transmit to the collector of customs at the port whence the
vessel cleared a certificate, under his hand and seal (Form 21), specifying the
seamen to whose discharge he has consented, and also those who may have died,
absconded, or been forcibly impressed into other service.-29 Stat. L. 688.
Paragraph 202 is amended to read as follows:

202. Seamen on fishing vessls.-Except as noted in these Regulations,
American seamen, as above defined, engaged on fishing vessels are to be regarded,
in respect to the laws applying to discharge, wages, extra wages, relief, and
transportation, in the same relation as seamen on other vessels.-3o Stat. L.

(1)

2
Paragraph 205 is amended by cancelling the title " Bond for return of sea-
men " and substituting therefor " Penalty for failure to return seamen," and by
substituting the word " person " for the word " seaman " in line ten.
Paragraph 2 20 is canceled.
Paragraph 221 is amended to read as follows:

221. Seamen to be reported .- When a seaman comes upon a consulate either
from another port, or by shipwreck, or in any manner otherwise than by dis-
charge from a vessel at the port, the consular officer will at once notify the
Comptroller General of the United States, State and other Departments Division,
of the fact, giving the name of the seaman, the date of arrival, the name of the
place whence he came, with the date and cause of his leaving such place, the name
of the vessel by which he came, and the name of the American vessel on which
he was last engaged. This information should be communicated immediately
and without waiting until the end of the quarter. (Form No. 126.)
Paragraph 224 is amended to read as follows :

224. Arrears of wages to be collected and reported .- It is the duty of the con-
sular officer to collect all arrears of wages that are due to the seaman at the time
of his discharge, and to report the same quarterly together with the extra wages
collected, to the Department of State (Form No. 124); and vouchers for wages
paid to a seaman, as prescribed in Form No. 164, must accompany the relief
accounts. The arrears of wages and extra wages are to be paid to the seaman,
and consular officers have no authority to retain them for the relief of the sea-
man.-R. S. Sec. 4581; 30 Stat. L. 759, Sec. i6; 38 Stat. L. r 85, Sec. 19.
Paragraph 245 is amended by inserting the word "undocumented" before
the word " American " in the second line of the paragraph.
Paragraph 248 is amended to read as follows:

248. Foreign sea men.-It is held that when a seaman, being a foreigner, who
has not declared his intention of becoming a citizen and served three years on a
merchant vessel, agreeably to an act approved May 9, 1918 (40 Stat. L. 544), is
shipped in a foreign port and is discharged in a foreign port, no extra wages are
to be collected-Fed. Cases 16oo2.
Paragraph 253 and all other paragraphs of the Regulations wherein the
term " Auditor for the State and other Departments " appears are amended by
cancelling therein the aforesaid term and substituting therefor the term "Comp-
troller General of the United States, State and Other Departments Division."
Paragraph 260 is amended to read as follows :

260. Seamen entitled to relief.-Seamen of the United States entitled to
relief when destitute are :

clauses.label: (i)
clauses.text:
(i) Merchant seamen, being citizens of the United States, or persons
coming under the provisions of an act approved May 9' 1918 (40 Stat. L. 544),
and who, at the time of applying for relief, are by habit and intent bona fide
members of the American merchant marine, although their last service may not
have been in an American vessel.

(2) Foreigners regularly shipped in an American vessel in a port of the
United States.
The following classes of seamen are to be considered as destitute and en-
titled to relief regardless of money they may have in possession or of wages due:

clauses.label: (t)
clauses.text:
(t) Seamen of the United States, formally discharged from American
vessels before a consular officer on account of injury or illness incapacitating them
for service.-R. S. 4581, amended; 30 Stat. L. 75 38 Stat. L. 1185.

(2) All seamen, regardless of nationality or port of shipment, who are from
shipwrecked American vessels. (Except seamen on fishing or whaling vessels
or yachts. 30 Stat. L. 764, Sec. 26.) R. S. 4526, amended; 30 Stat. L. 755.
Paragraph 262 is amended to read as follows :

262. Conditions of relief .- Be fore granting relief, a consular officer should
satisfy himself that the applicant is an American seaman as already defined,
and that he is entitled to relief under the statutes, usages, and decisions herein-
before referred to, and that he is destitute. A seaman can not be regarded as

3
destitute when he has any arrears of wages or extra wages, or is earning his own
living, unless he comes within the provisions contained in Paragraph 260 above.
The question of fact whether a seaman is or is not destitute is one to be deter-
mined by the consular officer to whom the seaman applies for relief, and the con-
sular officer's decision will, in the absence of fraud, be conclusive.--3 Comp.
Dec. 40.
Paragraph 264 is amended by adding at the end thereof the words "or by
deserting without cause."
Paragraph 266 is amended to read as follows:

266. Deserters and seamen who a re forced to leave their vesses.-An American
citizen serving as seaman on an American vessel is entitled to relief if destitute
in a foreign port, notwithstanding he may have deserted without cause or comes
upon the consulate otherwise irregularly.-3 Suxnn. i i 5s.-A foreigner under like
circumstances is not entitled to relief. (Paragraph 25,0.) When relief is applied
for by a deserter, it is the duty of the consular officer to ascertain clearly and
satisfactorily, before granting it, that he is justly entitled to it, but, in all such
cases, care should be taken that the provisions for the relief of destitute seamen
should not be allowed to operate as an incitement to desertion. Consuls should
exercise great care in examining and weighing the merits of each case, in order
that abuses may not occur. If, however, in applying for relief, an applicant
complains that he was compelled to leave the vessel because the voyage was
continued contrary to agreement, or that the vessel was badly provisioned or
unseaworthy, or that he was cruelly treated by the officers, the consular officer
shall investigate carefully the complaint, and if he is satisfied of the truth and
justice thereof, he shall discharge the seaman and require the master to pay such
seaman one month's wages over and above the wages due at the time of the dis-
charge, and to provide him with adequate employment on board some other
vessel, or provide him with passage to the port from which hie was shipped, or to
the most convenient port of entry in the Uni ted States, or to a port agreed to by
the seaman. R. S., Sec. 4583; 30 Stat. L., 760. If the vessel shall have left
the port, and the consular officer is satisfied that the case is within the provisions
of the statute, the facts should be reported to the Department of State.
Paragraph 268 is amended to read as follows:

268. Whaling vessel orders.-Orders given by masters of whaling vessels to
American seamen shipped "by the lay ", and discharged before the end of the
voyage, for the said seamen's shares of the catch up to the date of discharge,
payable at the end of the voyage, are understood to be of little or no value at
the time and place of discharge, and are therefore unavailable for expenditure
by the seamen in their own behalf. Discharged seamen who have no means of
subsistence at hand other than these orders are for that reason destitute, and
fit subjects for relief by the Government, notwithstanding the orders and their
contingent prospective value.
Relief out of Government funds is not to be given until the seaman is
destitute, having exhausted his own available resources (unless he is discharged
for injury or illness incapacitating him for service) ; but when given it is a pure
gr:atuity, without expectation of indemnity from subsequent acquisitions or
realizations of the seaman. If, therefore, these orders can not be utilized by
seamen in defraying the cost of their subsistence and other necessaries, or for
their transportation, at the time and place of discharge, they should be delivered
to the seamen to whom they are respectively payable; or, at the request of a
seaman, his order may be sent to the Department of State to be kept for him,
and subject to his call. In no case should it be taken from him and sent to
the Department for collection for the benefit of the Government.
Paragraph 269 is amended to read as follows:

269. Stowaways.-Any person who conceals himself on board a vessel and is
discovered when the vessel is at sea, although he has been put on duty as a
seaman, can be put on shore at the first available port unless he has been signed

4
on the ship's articles, in which case he is entitled to the benefits accorded sea-
men by the Navigation Laws and the shipping articles.
Unless the stowaway has been signed on the articles, it is not the duty of
the consular officer to afford relief to him as a destitute seaman in case he is
put ashore, and the expenses of relief under such circumstances are not allowed.
Paragraph 2 74 is amended to read as follows :

274. Vouchers for relief-Proper vouchers for the board, subsistence,
clothing, medical attendance and medicines, and any expenditures for the
relief of destitute seamen must be taken in every case. (Forms Nos. 95, 96,
97, and 98.) The vouchers for board and medical attendance should show the
name of the seaman, the time of subsistence or treatment, giving the date of
beginning and termination and the rate per day or week, and, whenever it is
practicable, the name of the ship from which and the place where the seaman
was discharged. Under the rules of the accounting officers of the United
States the receipts for clothing, necessaries, and supplies, given by a seaman
making his mark, or otherwise, should be witnessed. The witness should be a
disinterested person, not a member of the firm furnishing the articles. The
accounts for the relief of seamen must be accompanied by a certificate of the
consul that he has neither received nor will receive, directly or indirectly, any
pecuniary or other advantage whatever from the expenditures set forth in the
accounts.
Paragraph 277 and all other paragraphs of the Regulations wherein the
term "Comptroller of the Treasury" appears are amended by cancelling therein
the aforesaid term and substituting therefor the term " Comptroller General of
the United States.'"
Paragraph 286 and all other paragraphs of the Regulations wherein provision
is made that drafts shall be "drawn upon the Secretary of the Treasury" are
amended by substituting therein the word " State " for the words " the Treas-
ury ", and all official drafts hereafter drawn by consular officers for whatever
purpose shall be drawn upon the Secretary of State.
Paragraph 291 is amended by striking out the words " maintenance and
transportation of destitute American seamen", and by substituting therefor the
following: "relief and protection of destitute American seamen"
Paragraph 301 is amended by striking out the words "of the bond for the
return of his crew" and substituting therefor the words "to return his crew ".
Paragraph 308 in canceled.
Paragraph 309 is canceled.
Paragraph 317 is amended to read as follows :

317. When provisions are reduced.-If, during a voyage, the allowance of
any of the provisions which any seaman is entitled to under section forty six
hundred and twelve of the Revised Statutes is reduced, except for any time
during which such seaman wilfully and without sufficient cause refuses or neg-
lects to perform his duty, or is lawfully under confinement for misconduct either
on board or on shore; or if it shall be shown that any of such provisions are, or
have been during the voyage, bad in quality or unfit for use, the seaman shall
receive, by way of compensation for such reduction or bad quality, according to
the time of its continuance, the following sums, to be paid to him in addition to
and to be recoverable as wages :
First. If his allowance is reduced by any quantity not exceeding one-third
of the quantity specified by law, a sum not exceeding 5o cents a day.
Second. If his allowance is reduced by more than one-third of such quan-
tity, a sum not exceeding $ i a day.
Third. In respect to bad quality, a sum not exceeding $i a day.
But if it is shown to the satisfaction of the court before which the case is
tried that any provisions, the allowance of which has been reduced, could not be
procured or supplied in sufficient quantities, or were unavoidably injured or
lost, or if by reason of its innate qualities any article becomes unfit for use and

5
that proper and equivalent substitutes were supplied in lieu thereof, the court
shall take such circumstances into consideration and shall modify or refuse
compensation, as the justice of the case may require.-R. S. Sec. 45s68; 30 Stat.
L. 759, Sec. 14. This paragraph shall not apply to fishing or whaling vessels
or yachts.-3o Stat. L. 759, Sec. 26.
Paragraph 320 is canceled.
Paragraph 322 is amended in the last sentence to read as follows :
"The official fee prescribed in the Tariff of United States Consular Fees
for settling estates is not chargeable for services required by this paragraph."
Paragraph 334 is amended to read as follows:

334. Bottonry and sale.-After the estimate of damage, the master may
endeavor to borrow on bottomry the necessary funds for repairs; and in case of
inability to do so, he may be forced to sell the vessel. If the necessary funds
are procured, and a bottomry bond is given and acknowledged before the con-
sular officer, Form No. 68 may be used.
Paragraph 339 is canceled.
Paragraph 342 is amended to read as follows :

342. Provisional certificates of registry.-Consular officers of the United
States and such other persons as may be designated by the President for the
purpose are authorized to issue provisional certificates of registry to vessels
abroad which have been purchased by citizens of the United States, including
corporations, as defined in section 4132, Revised Statutes, as amended by the
Panama Canal Act, and an act of August eighteenth, nineteen hundred and
fourteen.
Such a provisional certificate shall entitle the vessel to the privileges of a
vessel of the United States in trade with foreign countries or with the Philippine
Islands and the Islands of Guam and Tutuila until the expiration of six months
from its date or until ten days after the vessel's arrival at a port of the United
States, whichever first happens, and no longer. On arrival at a port of the
United States the vessel shall become subject to the laws relating to officers,
inspection, and measurement, as amended by the act of August eighteenth,
nineteen hundred and fourteen.
The Secretary of Commerce shall prescribe the conditions in accordance
with which such provisional certificates shall be issued, and the manner in
which they shall be surrendered in exchange for certificates of registry at ports
of the United States. (Paragraph 346.)
The form of such provisional certificate shall be prescribed by the Com-
missioner of Navigation and shall include the name of the ship and of the master,
time and place of purchase and the names of purchasers, and the best particulars
respecting her tonnage, build, description, and inspection or survey which the
consular officer is able to obtain.
Copies of such provisional certificates shall be forwarded as soon as prac-
ticable by the issuing officer to the Commissioner of Navigation through the
P partment of State. No provisional certificates of registry shall be issued by
a consular officer except under, and in accordance with, specific instructions of
the Department of Commerce.
Paragraph 343 is amended to read as follows :

343. Operation of vessels structurally unable to proceed to the United States.-
In order to enable the American owners of vessels purchased abroad which are
unable to proceed to the United States to protect their rights, if molested or
questioned, a consular officer may lawfully make record of the bill of sale in his
office, authenticate its execution, and deliver to the purchaser a certificate to
that effect; certifying, also, that the owner is a citizen of the United States.
Before granting such a certificate, the consular officer shall obtain authorization
from the Department of State, and shall require the tonnage of the vessel to be
duly ascertained in pursuance of law and inserted in the description of the vessel
in his certificate. (Form No. 35.) These facts thus authenticated, if the transfer

6
is in good faith, enttite the vessel to protection as the lawful property of a citizen
of the United States; and the authentication of the bill of sale and of citizenship
shall be prima face proof of such good faith.
Paragraph 346 is amended to read as follows:

346. Conditions under which provisional certificates ofJ registry and Form 35Imay be issued .- When a consular officer shall have satisfied himself, after the
investigation with which he is charged, that the sale of a vessel is not fictitious
and is made in good faith, and that the purchaser is a citizen of the United
States, he should forward the results of his investigation to the Department for
instructions relative to granting a provisional certificate of American registry,
or a certificate showing that the bill of sale has been noted in the consulate and
that the purchaser is an American citizen. (Paragraph 342.)
Paragraph 348 is amended to read as follows:

348. Disabilities of foreign-built vessels.-All foreign-built vessels admitted
to American registry, owned on February i, 1920, by persons citizens of the
United States, and all foreign-built vessels owned by the United States at the

of the Act of Congress, approved June 10, 1922, relative to increased pay for

~,Executive Order of July 1, 1922, is amended by adding the following :

clauses.label: (i)
clauses.text:
(i) " Duty involving flying" is defined as any duty which requires partici-pation in flights in aircraft as prescribed in Paragraph 9 of the Executive
Order of July 1, 1922. The personnel of the Air Service of the Army
and of the aeronautical organizations of the Navy, Marine Corps, and
Coast Guard must be available at all times to render flying service. The
rated personnel of these branches or services, and, subject to the limi-
tations imposed by Section 20 of Act of June io, 1922, such other per-
sonnel assigned or attached to these branches or services as the respective
chiefs thereof designate for such duty, are and shall be, required to
participate in flights as prescribed in said Paragraph 9 and this duty
shall be duty involving flying and shall be performed in addition to
any other duty or duties to which such personnel may be detailed. All
of this personnel thus placed on duty involving flying shall participate
in aerial flights as prescribed in said Paragraph 9, unless prevented from
so doing by sickness or injury, or unless specifically relieved from the
performance of such flying duty by the orders of competent authority.

(2) An "aerial flight" is defined as a journey in an aircraft and such aerial
flight will begin when the aircraft leaves the ground or water and will
terminate when again at rest on the ground or water.

(3) Compliance with Paragraph 9 of the E xecutive Order of July r, 1922,
shall constitute frequent and regular flights within the meaning of the
Act of June 30, 1922, (Public 259), 67th Congress.
(4.) Authorized leaves of absence of personnel detailed to duty involving
flying shall not suspend such detail for pay purposes.

(5) "Travel by air" is defined as a journey in an aircraft made by orders of
competent authority and which requires one or more landings away
from the starting point.

(6) A "continuous journey by air" is defined as any journey performed in
an aircraft under the orders of competent authority, from and return
to the place of permanent station or to other final destination named
in the orders, which requires one or more landings, provided that the
stop, except that due to the causes set forth below, in any one locality
does not exceed seventy-two hours.

(7) A "necessary delay" incident to one or more of the following conditions
is a delay during a continuous voyage:

clauses.text:
Erecutive 4 Orer
MONTANA - ''
The temporary withdrawal made by Executive Order of November 23,
1914 (No. 2092), under the Act of June 25, 1910 (36 Stat., 847), as amended, of
the SE /, Sec. 4, T. 6 N., R. 12 E., M. P. M., Montana, for use by the Forest
Service as Big Elk ranger station in the administration of the Absaroka National
Forest, is hereby revoked.
It is hereby ordered pursuant to Public Resolution No. 29, approved
February 14, 1920, as amended by Public Resolution No. 36, approved Janu-
ary 21, 1922, that the above described area, subject to valid rights, shall be
opened only to entry under the homestead and desert land laws by qualified
ex-service men of the war with Germany, under the terms and conditions of
said resolutions, and the regulations issued thereunder, for a period of ninety-
one days beginning with the twenty-eighth day from and after the date of this
order, and thereafter to appropriation under any public land law applicable
thereto by the general public: Provided that, in the absence of a prior adverse
right, the preference accorded the State of Montana under the provisions of
the Act of Congress approved March 3, 1893 (27 Stat., 592), will attach immedi-
ately upon the restoration of such lands to selection and entry under the general
land laws, as herein provided, and continue for sixty days.
Subsequent to this order and prior to the date of restoration to general
disposition as herein provided, no rights may be acquired to said lands by
settlement in advance of entry, or otherwise, except strictly in accordance
herewith.

Executive (Other
WHEREAS, pursuant to the Act of Congress entitled "An Act Providing
additional hospital facilities for patients of the Bureau of War Risk Insurance
and of the Federal Board for Vocational Education, Division of Rehabilitation,
and for other purposes", approved March 4, 1921, the Secretary of the Treasury
has acquired for the use of the Public Health Service certain properties for the
construction of hospitals for tuberculous ex-service men;
AND WHEREAS Section 9 of the Act of Congress entitled "An Act to estab-
lish a Veterans' Bureau and to improve the facilities and service of such Bureau,
and further to amend and modify the War Risk Insurance Act ", approved
August 9' 1921, provides that:
" Section 9. The director, subject to the general directions of the President,
shall be responsible for the proper examination, medical care, treatment, hos-
pitalization, dispensary and convalescent care, necessary and reasonable after
care, welfare of, nursing, vocational training, and such other services as may be
necessary in the carrying out of the provisions of this Act, and for that purpose
is hereby authorized to utilize the now existing or future facilities of the United
States Public Health Service, the War Department, the Navy Department,the
Interior Department, the National Homes for Disabled Volunteer Soldiers, and
such other governmental facilities as may be made available for the purposes
set forth in this Act; and such governmental agencies are hereby authorized and
directed. to furnish such facilities, including personnel, equipment, medical,
surgical, and hospital services and supplies as the Director may deem necessary
and advisable in carrying out the provisions of this Act, in addition to such
governmental facilities as are hereby made available. * *"
AND WHEREAS said Section 9 further provides that:
" In the event that there is not sufficient Government hospital and other
facilities for the proper medical care and treatment of beneficiaries under this
Act, and the Director deems it necessary and advisable to secure additional
Governmental facilities, he may, within the limits of appropriations made for
carrying out the provisions of this paragraph, and with the approval of the
President, improve or extend existing governmental facilities, or acquire addi-
tional facilities by purchase or otherwise. Such new property and structures as
may be so improved, extended, or acquired shall become part of the permanent
equipment of the Veterans' Bureau or of some one of the now existing agencies
of the Government, including the War Department, Navy Department, Interior
Department, Treasury Department, the National Homes for Disabled Volunteer
Soldiers, in such a way as will best serve the present emergency, taking into
consideration the future services to be rendered the veterans of the World War,
including the beneficiaries under this Act."
Now, THEREFORE, By virtue of the authority vested in me by said law, I
direct that the property in O'Hara Township, Allegheny County, Pennsylvania,
known as the Hall property at Aspinwall, near Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania, com-
prising 147,543 acres, being bounded on the north by Township road, on the
east by Squaw Run, on the south by land of the City of Pittsburgh and land of
the Peoples Savings and Trust Company of Pittsburgh, and on the west by land
of the Delafield Land Company, together with an easement or right of way
thirty feet in width over lands of the Peoples Savings and Trust Company of
Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania, affording access to the Freeport road, heretofore
acquired from the Peoples Savings and Trust Company of Pittsburgh by the
Secretary of the Treasury for the use of the Public Health Service, is hereby
transferred to the United States Veeas Bureau and shall on and after the
date of this order be under the jurisdiction of and shall operate under the super-
vision, management and control of the Director of the United States Veterans'
Bureau.

Executive Orber
WXHEREAS there are large seepages of petroleum along the Arctic Coast of
Alaska and conditions favorable to the occurrence of valuable petroleum fields
on the Arctic Coast and,
WHEREAS the present laws designed to promote development seem imper-
fectly applicable in the region because of its distance, difficulties, and large
expense of development and,
WHEREAS the future supply of oil for the Navy is at all times a matter of
national concern,
Now, THEREFORE, 1, WARREN G. HARDING, President of the United
States of America, by virtue of the power in me vested by the laws of the United
States, do hereby set apart as a Naval Petroleum Reseve all of the public
lands within the following described area not now covered by valid entry, lease
or application : .-.. 1
Commencing at the most northwestern extremity of the point of land shown
on the maps of Alaska as Icy Cape, approximately lat. 700 21', long. 1610 46';
thence extending in a tru-, south course to the crest of the range of mountains
forming the watershed between the Noatak River and its northern tributaries
and the streams flowing into the Arctic Ocean; thence eastward along the
crest of this range of mountains to a peak at the head of the northermost of the
two eastern forks of Midas Creek (Pl. 1, U.S.G.S., Bull. 536), at approximately
lat. 670 50', long. 156°08o'; thence in a true north course to a point at the highest
high water on the western or right bank of the Colville River; thence following
said highest highwater mark downstream along said Colville River and the west-
ern bank of the most western slough at its mouth to the highest highwater mark
on the Arctic coast. From here, following the highest highwater mark west-
ward to the point of beginning.
The coast line to be followed shall be that of the ocean side of the sandspits
and islands forming the barrier reefs and extending across small lagoons from
point to point, where such barrier reefs are not over three miles off sore, except
in the case of Plover Islands, from Point Tangent to Point Barrow (P. 3,
U.S.G.S., P.P. ioj), long. approximately 154° 5', where it shall be the highest
highwater mark on the outer shore of the islands forming the groups and extend-
ing between the most adjacent points of these islands and the sandspits at either
end. In cases where the barrier reef is over three miles off shore the boundary
shall be the highest highwater mark of the coast of the mainland.
Said lands to be so reserved for six years for classification, examination,
and preparation of plans for development and until otherwise ordered by the
Congress or the President.
The reservation hereby established shall be for oil and gas only and shall
not interfere with the use of the lands or waters within the area indicated for
any legal purpose not inconsistent therewith.

~-Eights coimmon/v quaranteed under treaties and con zcntions.-The
fundamental rights and privileges of consular officers depend upon the prin-

rights and privileges are also specifically guaranteed to them by treaties. The
several consular treaties and conventions of the United States with foreign
powers are, or should be, on file in every consular office, and in each case the
consul must examine the proper treaty for detailed information. The Depart-
ment of State must necessarily trust to the discretion of the consul, on the one
hand, not to permit his rights to be invaded without protest, and, on the other
hand, niot to claim what he can not maintain. When consular officers feel
that they' have reason to believe that tihe rights secured to them by treaty
have been infringed, a report should he promptly submitted to the Department
of State and to the supervising consul general, if there be one, or to the AXmerican
diplomatic representative. The report should set forth in full the facts showing
the infringement.
Through treaties with certain countries the United States has secured to its
consular officers therein such rights as: the privileges, exemptions. and immuni-
ties granted the most favored nation; the inviolability of the consular office,
dwelling, and archives; the right to exemption from arrest except for crimes
under the local law, to exemption from taxation, military billeting, military
service, and the obligation to appear as a witness; the right to correspond with
local authorities in case of any infraction of treaty'; the right to place the national
arms and the name of the consulate on the consular office or dwelling, and to
fly the national flag on the office or dwelling; the right to take depositions, and
to adjust all matters pertaining to wrecks and salvage: the right to be informed
by the local authorities of the death of citizens of the United States who die
intestate or without heirs, and to take charge of and administer on property left
by them; thle right, in tile absence of a diplomatic representative, to make req~ui-
sition for the surrender of fugitives from justice; and, in a few countries, the
right to exercise judicial power in civil or criminal cases, or both.
Not all treaties provide for the same rights, and with some nations the United
States has 110 consular convention whatever. I t is, therefore, the duty of every
consular officer thoroughly to familiarize himself with the terms of whatever
treaty or treaties may exist between the Unted States anld the government from
which he holds his exequatur.

commander of the squadron to send a boat ashore, with an officer on board, who
shall call upon the consular officer, notify him of the arrival of the squadron,
and tender him a passage to the fla'gshiip at such time as he may select. It is
the duty of the consular officer to accept the invitation and visit the flagship
as early, as convenient, which must be within a period not exceeding twenty
four hours, and to ..ender his official services to the commander.
Paragraph i1i0 is amended to read as follows:
ii10. Commftanders of .lhips of wa,.---When .a ship of war of the United
States visits a foreign port where there is a consular officer, it is the duty of
the commander thereof, if not a flag officer, to pay the first visit in person to a
consul general, and to tender him passage to his ship. If the commander be a
flag officer, or if the consular officer be of lower grade than a consul general, it
is the duty of the commander to send a boat ashore, with an officer on board,
to visit the consular officer and tender him a passage to the ship at such time as
he may select. It is the duty of the consular officer to accept the invitation to
visit the commander or return his visit, as circumstances may require, within
a period not exceeding twenty four hours, and to tender to him his official
services.
Paragraph YI is amended to read as follows:
I I I. Sal uts-A cons~ul general is entitled once while a naval force or vessel
is in port to a salute of eleven guns; a consul to a salute of seven guns; and a
vice consul, or consular ageiit, when hie is the only representative of the United
States at the post, to a salute of five guns. The salute may he fired either while
the consular officer is on hoard whichi is unusual), or while he is being conveyed
from the vessel to the shore. In the latter case lie will stand .and face the
vessel, and at the end of the salute acknowledge it by raising his hat.
Article IX, entitled "Correspondence with the Department of State"~ is
canceled, and the following substituted therefor.
Article IX.
CORRESPONDENCE AND REPORTS.

114. Correspontdentce ont public mutters-A consular officer may not corres-
pond on public matters with any other official or branch of the Government of
the United States than the Departmnt of State, except as expressly provided
in paragraph 18.
zI. 5. Secretary of .State odli to be addressed-All communications to the
Department of State must be addressed to the Secretary of State. Recourse to
private letters to the Secretary or to other officers of the Department of State
upon topics relating to official business is disapproved. Communications in
relation to the public business must always be in the form of regular despatches
to the Secretary.
i 16. (*o ondetw~l coinin utic(tionts. -Despa tchcs regarded as especially of a
reserved or secret nature should be conspicuously marked "Confidential'" on the
top of the first page. «"here onie or niore paragraphs of a despatch seem to
require precauitioni against p)ublicityv, ia red line may be dIrawn on the margin
opposite to mark them, and the word "Confidential "plainly written outside
this line. TIhe Secretary of State, however, reserves the ultimate right to decide
whether the suggested reserve is nitcessary ill the public interest.
11 7. Corrcspontdecc of suo(lllIs-h official correspondence of consuls
assigned to, or on detail in, consulates general or consulates, vice consuls, inter-
preters, consular assistants, and student interpreters will be submitted to the
examination oJf the principal consulfar officers to whom they~ are subordinate, or
to whose office they are assigned~. Consular agents are not authorized to address
the D~epartmenit of State directly, or to miake their reports or returns, except
through their respective superio .

4
i 1. lWithz whom direct correspondence is permitted-As exceptions to the
general rule stated in paragraph 1 14, a consular officer may correspondl directly
on public matters with the following:
i. The American diplomatic representative in the country in which he is
assigned or detailed and other American consular officers.
~.Military and naval officers of the United States, serving abroad, with
whom it may be necessary to communicate immediately information of inmpor-
tance.

3. Public health surgeons, special agents of the Treasury Department,
agents of the United States Shipping Board, and representatives of the Depart-
ments of Commerce and Agriculture, on duty in foreign countries, with whom

-F. The Comptroller General of the United States, on matters pertaining to

a. Collectors of customs and appraisers, on matters relating to invoices

S. United States despatch agents.

spond directly with p~riv'ate citizens in the Unlited States, and others, respecting

Xxecutive ®rber.
The Consular Regulations are hereby amended as follows:
A new paragraph, to be known as 422 ", is. added after paragraph 422, to
read as follows: Cf./
' 41" .221 . Registration oj births of A mericans.-Consular officers are required,
upon application, to record the birth of American children abroad. They should
impress upon American citizens resident in their respective districts the desir-
ability and importance of a prompt registry of such births. The consul will
1yC , record the name and sex of the child, the date and place of birth, the names
and residence of the parents, together with such other facts concerning them as
will fully establish the identity and citizenship of the child. He will furnish
the registrant a copy of the record, and also transmit a copy thereof to t~e
Department of State. No fee shall be charged for the registration of a birth,
nor for the issuance of a copy of the record thereof.
Paragraph 429 is amended to read as follows:

429. Form for supplies-A form of requisition for office supplies, and a
schedule of such supplies as are usually carried in stock, are furnished to con-
sular officers by the Department. Requisitions for supplies should describe
the articles called for by schedule number, as well as by name, and the quanl-
tities desired are to he stated in figures, as per schedule, and in the order indicated
therein. If less than an original package is required, the quantity should he
stated in fractions thereof. The requisition should be carefully drawn, with
due regard to economy, and should cover as far as possible a supply for a year
or half year.
Seals, coats of arms, and other articles not mentioned on the schedule
should be added at the end of the requisition, or, if necessary, on a separate
sheet accompanying the same.
No despatch is necessary in transmitting these requisitions to the
Department.
Paragraph 431 is amended to read as follows:
431i. Inventory required-Every consular officer in charge of an office shall
keep on record in the office and furnish the Department with a detailed inventory
of all government property in his custody, including record books and archives.
An inventory must be submitted to the Department by the officer in
charge upon the establishment of a new consular office; upon instructions from
the Department or from the consul general at large acting under authority of
the Department, when the inventory previously prepared is in improper form;
or upon the transfer of an office from one consular officer to another.
A retiring consular officer will not be given a certificate of non-indebtedness
to th1c Government until the provisions of the regulations respecting inventories
have been fully complied with.
No government property shall be disposed of nor removed from the inven-
tory without the authorization, in advance, of the Department. The penal
code of the United States (35 Stat. L. 111i2.) provides: "Whoever, having the
custody of any record, proceeding, map, book, document, paper or other things
specified in the preceding section (the preceding section of the statute specifies
any such things which may be "in any public office'), shall willfully and unlaw-

2
fully conceal, remove, mutilate, obliterate, falsify or destroy any such record,
proceeding, map, book, document, paper, or thing, shall be lined not more than
two thousand dollars, or imprisoned not more than three years, or both, and shall
moreover forfeit his office and be forever afterward disqualified from holding
any office under the Government of the United States."
Paragraph 432 is amended to read as follows:

432. Preparation andl recording of inventory.-The inventory must be pre-
pared with the typewriter, on form 223, in three sections, designated respectively:
"Furniture and Furnishings"; "Reference Books"; and "Record Books and
Archives ". It shall be signed and certified as correct by the officer preparing it.
After being prepared, the inventory must be copied in the "Miscellaneous
Record Book", sufficient space being left at the end of each section to permit of
future entries upon supplementary inventories. Having been once recorded in
correct form it is not necessary to recopy it in succeeding volumes of the " Mis-
cellaneous Record Book", but a reference should always be made in the current
volume to the one in which the inventory appears.
After being recorded in the manner stated above a copy of the inventory
must be forwarded to the Department, a copy filed in the office files, and a third
copy kept on hand for the use of the consul general at large in making his in-
spection.
Paragraph 433 is amended to read as follows:

433. Transmtiss'iont of inventory upon transfer of office.-Upon the transfer or
departure of the officer in charge of a consulate, except on leave of absence, a
copy of the inventory, corrected to date and signed jointly by the outgoing and
incoming officer, shall be transmitted to the Department. When there is an
ad interim charge of an office, pending the arrive - an officer permanently
assigned to it, the inventory should be duly prepared and signed jointly by the
outgoing officer and the officer temporarily in charge; but it should be retained
for examination, for any necessary notation, and for the signature of the newly
assigned officer, and be by him forwarded to the Department as soon after
his arrival as possible. Should lie find any discrepancies between the number
and descriptions of the articles listed in the inventory and those actually on hand,
lie will report the matter to the Department, and submit a statement by the
temporary officer relative thereto.
A new paragraph, to be known as 433 '2, is added after paragraph 433, to read
as follows:
433'i Supplementari' inventory-During such time as an officer continues in
charge of a post, a correct inventory having previously been submitted, he will
prepare and transmit to the Department at the end of each fiscal year a stupple-
mentary inventory including all property acquired, and all records or files added
to the archives during such fiscal year.
Paragraph 440 is amended to read as follows:

440. Relative ranik-The order of official precedence in the service is as
follo.vs: (i) Consuls General; (2) consuls; (3) vice consuls de carri~re, and
interpreters; (4) consular assistants amid student interpreters when com-
missioned as vice consuls; (5) vice consuls not of career; (6) consular assistants
and student interpreters when not commissioned as vice consuls; (7) consular
agents.

3
Paragraph 445 is amended to read as follows:

445. hatter transmitted in. Govern inent pouches.-The following matter may
be transmitted in government pouches, and none other, except as may be
specially authorized by the Department of State from time to time.

(1) Despatches, official communications, reports, printed matter and
packages for the Department of State or for transmission to other departments
or branches of the Government.

(2) Letters, communications, reports, printed matter and packages for
individuals or firms required to be handled in the performance of official duties.
Matter corning under this head should not bear postage.

(3) Except when the United States is at wvar, private letters of consular
officers and members of their immediate families, their assistants and clerks, if
of American nationality, to their families and friends in the United States;
also private letters of representatives of any other branch of the Government
of the United States, their assistants and clerks, if of American nationality. On
all matter coming tinder this head full foreign postage must be prepaid in the
same manner as if it were forwarded in the open mail. Postage stamps of the
United States must not be used on such matter.
Paragraph 446 is canceled.
Paragraph 447 is canceled.
Paragraph 454 is canceled.
Paragraph 455 is canceled.
Paragraph 458 is canceled.
Paragraph 459 is canceled.
Paragraph 461 is amended to read as follows:
.,61. Use of the telera/h.-The use of the telegraph at the expense of the
Government is restricted to cases of urgency, and to those in which some injury
to the public interests would result from delay. It is not permitted in the
ordinary business of a consulate, or in communicating with the Department
of State, except when justified by the importance and urgency of the case, or
when it is done under instructions from the Department.
Applications by telegraph or cable for leave of absence andl telegraphic
replies thereto will generally be at the expense of the consular officer.
WVhenever possible tclcgrams should be sent in code for the purpose of
economy, even if tihe nature of the message does not otherwise require it.
Extreme care must be exercised to observe the regulations governing the use of
departmental codes set forth in the introductions to those books.
Telegrams of a non-oflicial character, dealing with matters of personal
interest to citizens of the United States, and sent at their solicitation, are to be
sent only at the expense of the citizens in question, and may be transmitted
only after prepayment of the charges, or satisfactory assurance of payment.
A telegraphic reply is charged to the person on whose account the original message
was sent.
Paragraph 462 is canceled.
Paragraph 463 is amended to read as follows:

463. Circulars of consular olftiers-All circulars issued over the signature
of a consular officer must he submitted to the Department of State and receive
its approval before publication.

4
Paragraph 464 is amended to read as follows:

464. Forms-The forms prescribed by the Department of State are to be
used in the cases to which they apply; and consular officers are forbidden to
alter them without permission and the approval by the Department of State of
the substitute offered. Suggestions for the improvement of forms are, however,
invited, and they will always receive consideration. Exact translation of Eng-
lish forms into the language of the country to which the consul is accredited is
not within this prohibition, where the local conditions require translation.
Paragraph 467 is amended to read as follows:

467. Conditions under which leave is granted.---Leave of absence is granted,
within statutory limitations, at the discretion of the President, acting through
the Secretary of State. Leaves are of two kinds, simple leave, and leave with
permission to visit the United States. The granting of a simple leave of absence
does not carry with it permission to return to the United States. A consular
officer must receive express permission to return, in order to entitle him to the
benefit of the statutory allowance of salary in transit.
Simple leave of absence with salary may be granted for not more than
thirty days in an) one year, except in the event of illness on the part of the
officer or a member of his family, or tinder other exceptional circumstances,
when simple leave with pay may be extended to a total of sixty days in on.
year, but no longer.
Leave of absence with permission to visit the United States for not to exceed
sixty days in any one calendar year may be granted with salary not oftener
than once in two years, except (r) in the case of consular officers in remote places,
who may be granted continuous leave covering parts of two successive years,
provided not to exceed sixty days is granted in either year; and (2) also in cases
where the health of officers requires that they should be absent from their posts,
when continuous leave not to exceed sixty days in either year may be granted
covering parts of two successive years. Whenever leave of absence is claimed
to be necessary on account of illness it is desirable that a certificate of the physi-
cian in attendance be forwarded to the Secretary of State.-R. S. Secs. 1740,

1742.
Leave of absence with permission to visit the United States is granted
exclusive of the time actually and necessarily occupied in transit by the most
direct route from the officers post to his residence in the United States and
return to his post. Salary for said transit period will be paid in addition to
the salary for the duration of the leave of absence.-R. S. Sec. 1742; 14 Comp.
Dec. 61. Salary will not be paid for more than one transit period in any one
year (io Comp. Dec. 465; 11 Comp. Dec. 123.) except that when all or part of
a transit period occurs in a calendar year other than that in which the leave of
absence was taken it will not impair the right of the consular officer to another
transit period during that calendar year if leave should be granted-i 4 Comp.
Dec. 61.
If consistent with the public interest leave of absence, for good reason, may
be granted for a longer time than that stipulated in the foregoing, hut without
compensation.-R. S. Sec. 1742.
Paragraph 470 is canceled.
Paragraph 471 is canceled.

5
Paragraph 472 is amended to read as follows:

472. Leave of absence of vice consuls, interpreters and consular assistants.-
The regulations in regard to leave of absence of consular officers (Paragraph 467)
are applicable to vice consuls de carriere, interpreters and consular :ssistalits.
Such officers should apply to the Secretary of State for leave, and ti eir applica-
tions should be transmitted through, and have the approval of, the principal
officer under whom they may be serving. In cases of emergency the principal
officer may grant them conditional leave, reporting the fact to the Secretary of
State for approval.
A vice consul not of career should make application for leave of absence to
his principal officer when the latter is at his post and in charge of the office, and
the principal officer may grant leave to the vice consul, reporting the fact to the
Secretary of State.
When a vice consul is in charge of an office he should apply to the Secretary
of State for leave in the same manner as if he were the principal, and if for any
reason, such as the non-arrival of another officer to relieve a vice consul, it should
become necessary to leave the office temporarily in charge of someone not
regularly appointed, the vice consul should obtain the approval of the Secretary
of State, and the name and authenticated signature of the person left in charge
should be forwarded immediately to the Secretary of State.
Leave of absence of vice consuls not of career, who receive compensation
as clerks (Paragraph 41) is subject to the limitations governing leave of absence
of clerks set forth in paragraph 473.
Paragraph 475 is canceled.
Paragraph 476 is amended to read as follows:

476. Interpreters and marshals.-An interpreter not of career, or a marshal,
should apply for leave of absence through the consular officer in charge of the
post. There is no provision of law for appointment by the consular officer of a
substitute to perform the duties of the absent interpreter or marshal and receive
his salary.-Bowlers ist. Comp. Dec. i68; 2 Conmp. Dec. 455
Paragraph 477 is amended to read as follows:

477. Time in. transit.-The Secretary of State is authorized to establish,
determine, and make public the maximum amount of time actually necessary
to make the transit between each consular post and the city of Washington,
and vice versa, and from time to time revise his decision in this respect; and the
allowance for time actually and necessarily occupied by each consular officer
who may be entitled to such allowance shall in no case exceed that for the time
thus established and determined, with the addition of the time usually occupied
by the shortest and most direct mode of conveyance from Washington to the
place of residence in the United States of such oficer-iS Stat. L. 70, Sec. 4.
With the exception of cases in which specific orders to the contrary are issued
in writing by the Department of State, the transit period within the meaning
of the statute will be construed to be the time actually and necessarily occupied
in making direct transit between the officers place of residence and his post of
duty, or vice versa.
Paragraph 478 is canceled.

6
Paragraph 482 is amended to read as follows:

482. Under Federal laws.-Every consular officer of the United States is
required, whenever application is made to him theref?'ir, within the limits of his
consulate, to administer to or take from any person any oath, affirmation,
affidavit or deposition, and to perform any other notarial act which any notary
public is required or authorized to perform within the United States.-34 Stat.
L. tox. Such acts, in order to be valid and effectual, must be certified by the
consul under his hand and seal of office.-R. S. Sec. 1750.
Paragraph 484 is amended to read as follows :

484. Fees for notarial services.--Consular officers shall charge for every
notarial act performed by them the appropriate fee prescribed by the President
under section 1745, Revised Statutes.
Paragraph 487 is amended to read as follows:

487. Patent application.-The oath to an application for a patent, to be
filed in the United States, when the applicant resides in a foreign country, may
be made before a consul of the United States or before a notary public, judge,
or magistrate having an official seal and authorized to administer oaths in the
foreign country in which the applicant may be, whose authority shall be proved
by the certificate of a diplomatic or consular officer of the United States.-R. S.

clauses.label: Sec. 4892.
clauses.text:
Sec. 4892.
Paragraph 488 is amended to read as follows:

488. Verification of powers to transfer notes and bonds of thme United States.-
Powers of attorney executed in a foreign country for the transfer of any note
or bond of the Government of the United States, or for the receipt of interest
thereon, shall be verified by the certificate and seal of a consular officer, if any
there be, at the place where the same is executed.
No fee is to be charged by consular officers for witnessing the execution
and taking the acknowledgment of assignments of notes and bonds of the
Government of the United States, or of powers of attorney to assign such notes
or bonds, or to collect the interest thereon.
A new paragraph, to be known as 488 J z, is added after paragraph 488, to
read as follows:

488. -. Authentication of pension papers-The Commissioner of Pensions is
authorized by statute to accept the declarations and other papers of pension
claimants residing in foreign countries made before a United States minister,
or consul, or other consular officer, or before some officer of that country duly
authorized to administer oaths for general purposes, and whose official character
and signature shall be duly authenticated by the certificate of a United States
minister, or consul, or other consular officer.-2 7 . Stat. L. 272, Sec. 2.
All United States officers now authorized to administer oaths are required
and directed to administer any and all oaths required to be made by pensioners
and their witnesses in the execution of their vouchers for their pensions free of
charge.-25 Stat. L. 782.

Executive Orber.
The Consular Regulations are hereby amended as follows:
Paragraph 491 is amended to read as follows:

491. Two classes of oticrs.-With respect to their compensation, consular
officers are divided into two classes, (r) those who are paid from appropriations
made annually by Congress, and (2) those who are paid no salary, but receive
their compensation in fees collected for official services and in payments from
the Treasury of the United States for services to American vessels and seamen.
Paragraph 492 is amended to read as follows:

492. Salaried officers.-Consuls general, consuls, vice consuls de carriere,
consular assistants, interpreters, and student interpreters, receiving salaries
fixed by law or executive order, are entitled to compensation at the rate of
their respective salaries, as follows :

(1) Beginning not prior to the date of the oath of office, for time occupied
in receiving instructions in the United States, or, by special direction of the
Department of State, at consulates general or consulates other than those to
which they shall have been appointed, not exceeding in all thirty days.-
R. S. Sec. 1740.

(2) For the time actually and necessarily occupied in transit, by the most
direct route, between the places of their residence and their posts, and vice
versa. (Paragraph 477.) This applies to transit from the United States, to
transit between posts when a transfer takes place, and to transit to the United
States at the termination of service, unless the officer dies, or is recalled for
malfeasance, or resigns in anticipation of such recall. The time during which
a consul may be unavoidably detained at his post while waiting for a conveyance
to tihe United States, or to another post, after delivering up the office, may be
included in his transit period provided he takes the first available means of
transportation. In the event that the appointee is not in the United States at
the time of appointment no allowance of salary will be mnadle except for the
period actually and necessarily occupied in transit in reaching his post of duty,
and the time which he may be especially directed by the Department of State
to spend at a consulate general or consulate other than that to which he shall
have been appointed receiving instructions in the performance of consular
duties, not exceeding thirty days.

(3) From the (late of entry upon official duty at their posts to the date
when they ease to perform the duties of the office. This provision extends
also to the time, after arrival at their posts. while awaiting the receipt of the
exequatur or permission ti, act.---R. S. Sec. 1740.
Paragraph 493 is canceled.
Paragraph 491 is canceled.
Paragraph 495 is amended by striking out the last sentence.
Paragraph 499 is canceled.

Paragraph 502 is amended to read as follows:

502. Salary during absence.-It is provided lby law that no consular officer
shall receive salary for the time during which he may be absent from his post,
by leave or otherwise, beyond the term of sixty days in the aggregate in any
one calendar year, but that the time equal to that usually occupied in going to
and from the United States, in case of the return on leave of such officer to the
United States, may be allowed in addition to the sixty days. A salaried officer
may accordingly receive the salary of his office for sixty days while absent from
his post on leave, and also for the time of transit both to and from his residence,
in case he visits the United States, as explained in paragraph 467. In case the
officer does not visit the United States no salary will be allowed after the expira-
tion of sixty days.-R. S. Sec. 1742; 12 Op. Att. Gen., 410.
Paragraph 50 is amended to read as follows:

505. Resignation in the United States.-The right to compensation of a
consular officer who resigns while in the United States on leave of absence
terminates with the date of the acceptance of the resignation, or the lapse of
his statutory leave, whichever first occurs.
Paragraph 506 is amended to read as follows:

506. Compensation of -vice consuls.-The salaries of vice consuls de carri~re
are set forth in paragraph 40, and are paid in the same manner as salaries of
consuls general andl consuls. For such time as they are lawfully authorized
to assume charge of consulates general or consulates vice consuls not of career
receive compensation at the rate of one half the salary provided by law for the
principal officers in charge of their respective posts. They receive no other
compensation unless they be also employed as clerks, in which case they receive
compensation for their services as clerks. Both vice consuls de carri~e and
vice consuls not of career, for such time as they are lawfully authorized to
assume charge of consulates general or consulates, whose salaries as subordinate
consular officers or employees are less than one half the salaries of the respective
principal officers in charge of such posts, are entitled to receive in addition to
their regular salaries or compensation, compensation equal to the difference
between such regular salaries or compensation and fifty per centum of the salaries
provided by law for the principal officers at such posts.
Vice consuls are entitled to salary when traveling to and from their posts,
or elsewhere, under the orders of the Secretary of State; and to salary while on
leave of absence subject to the law governing leaves of absence. (Para-
graph 467.)
Paragraph 509 is amended to read as follows:

509. (Compe nsation of student interpreters.--Student interpreters receive.
compensation, upon appointment as such, at the rate of $15o0 per annum.
They are also provided with tuition and quarters free. After acquiring a knowl-
edge of the language of the country and passing the first examination for promo-
tion, usually at the end of the second year of service, they are promoted to be
junior interpreters, or vice consuls de carri-He of Class III, with a compensa-
tion of $250o per annum. After passing the second examination for promo-
tion, usually at the end of the third or fourth year, they are promoted to be
senior interpreters, or vice consuls de carriere of Class I, with a compensation
of $3000 per annum. They are thereafter eligible for promotion without
further examination to the grade of consul of Class VI.

3
Paragraph 511 is amended to read as follows:

511. Corn pensatiwn of consular assistants.-Consular assistants appointed
by the President receive salaries according to the following schedule:
First year............. to
Second year............. $1650
Third year.............. $r8oo
Fourth year............. $200
They receive their salaries from the date they begin to discharge the duties towhich they are assigned by the President, which date is usually simultaneous
with that on which they take the oath of offce.-R. S. Secs. 1704, 170.5; 35 Stat.
L. ISO, Sec. 5~; 40 Stat. L. 134

51i6, Fees applicable to salaries.-Consls who are compensated by salaries
appropriated annually by Congress are authorized to pay themselves from the
fees they may collect if these shall be sufficient for the purpose. If not sufficient,
a draft may be drawn at the end of each quarter for the deficiency, or for the
whole quarter's salary, as the case may be. In all cases drafts for salary of
consuls should be drawn upon the Secretary of State.

of each quarter, and for amounts then due, and must be preceded or accompanied
by the corresponding accounts and vouchers. In case of need, however, salary
may be drawn before the end of the quarter, but not in a greater amount than is

of receipts from fees and the amount of salary accrued to the date of draft must

Executive ether
Transit and Harbor Regulations for The Panama Canal and Approaches
Thereto, Including All Waters Unde.r Its Jurisdiction.
By virtue of the authority vested in me by law it is ordered that the follow-
ing Transit and Harbor Regulations for The Panama Canal and Approaches
Thereto, including All Waters under its Jurisd tittn, ems, annd they are hereby,
3( adopted:
I. OPERATION AND NAVIGATION. '.

1. GENERAL.
Section I. These rules shall apply to all waters which are now or may
hereafter be under the jurisdiction of the Canal Zone Government.

clauses.label: Section 2.
clauses.text:
Section 2. Any person violating any of the provisions of the rules and
regulations established hereunder, shall be deemed guilty of a misdemeanor,
and, upon conviction thereof, shall, except where otherwise stated, be punished
by a fine not exceeding one hundred dollars ($roo.oo), or by imprisonment in
jail not exceeding thirty days, or by both such fine and imprisonment.

clauses.label: Section 3.
clauses.text:
Section 3. The Canal authorities may deny any vessel passage through the
Canal the cargo of which is of such a nature that it might, in any way, endanger
the locks, wharves, equipment, or any part of the Canal, by being explosive or
highly inflammable. The further right is reserved to them to impose such safety
regulations as they may see fit upon any such vessel while in Canal waters.

clauses.label: Section 4.
clauses.text:
Section 4. Vessels whose cargoes consist of high explosives should, before
leaving their ports of departure, when practicable, obtain permission from the
Canal authorities to use the Canal. In requesting such permission, the character
and approximate amount of explosives should be stated, the ports of departure
and destination, name of ship and party to whom consigned. This may be done
by mail or cable. In general, permission will not be refused, but these precau-
tions are taken to safeguard the Canal's interests. Vessels loaded with volatile
crude oil products must obtain permissioli to pass through after arrival, and this
will be granted unless there be some exceptionally good reason to the contrary.

clauses.label: Section 5.
clauses.text:
Section 5. Vessels carrying explosives consigned to ports beyond the ports
of the Canal Zone will not be allowed alongside the wharves while such explosives
are on board. Vessels having explosives consigned to Canal Zone ports must
obtain special permission from the Port Captain before they will be allowed
alongside the wharves, and must discharge such explosives before handling any
other cargo. Each instance will be handled upon its individual merits.

clauses.label: Section 6.
clauses.text:
Section 6. In aay case where the condition of the cargo, hull, or machinery
of a vessel is such that 4L is liable to endanger or obstruct the Canal, permission
to enter or pass through may be refused until steps have been taken to remedy
the defect.

clauses.label: Section 7.
clauses.text:
Section 7. Vessels are towed through the locks by electric locomotives,
using x t 4-inch, steel wire towing lines. Normally, the number of locomotives
used is as follows;
Length of vesel p. p.l
in feet No. of locomotives.
UP to 349 4
350 to 499 6
Soo and over 8
These numbers are subject to change, due to other conditions, such as list, trim,
or peculiar construction of a ship. In all cases the Canal pilot on board deter-
mines the number to be used.
I- /,,(

clauses.label: Section 8.
clauses.text:
Section 8. For each towing wire used the ship shall be fitted with a heavy
closed chock and a heavy pair of bitts, capable of withstanding a strain of
50,000 pounds on the towing wire at any angle. The forward and after chocks
should lbe as near the stem and stern, respectively, as they can conveniently be
located. For 6-locomotive ships there shall be a chock on each side near amid-
ships, and for 8-locomotive ships, two additional chocks on each side, one about
one-third the ship's length abaft thie bow and the other the same distance
forward of the stern.

clauses.label: Section 9.
clauses.text:
Section 9. The most suitable installations for the bow and stern towing
chocks are large chocks set thwartships right in the stem and stern, respec-
tivelv. These to lbe double the size and strength given above. Both bow wires
and both stern wires are run through such chocks.
Section io. The leads from chocks to bitts shall be short, straight and fair.
Section i i. While a vessel is being locked up, she shall be tied up to the
lock walls with manila mooring lines, one on each bow and one on each quarter,
in addition to the towing wires; when being locked down, these lines shall be
clear for In'ning and hea\ :ng lines passed to the wall.

clauses.label: Section 12.
clauses.text:
Section 12. 'V~wo deck hands for each locomotive wire are placed on board
such vessel, other thin men of war, at the terminal port prior to transit, to
assist the crew in handling the towing wires in the locks. An appropriate
charge is made for the services of these men.

clauses.label: Section 13.
clauses.text:
Section 13. The Canal authorities may dispatch vessels through the Canal
in any order and at any time they may see fit; priority of arrival ait a terminal
does not give any vessel the right to pass through the Canal ahead of another
that may arrive later, although this will be a consideration in determining the
order of passage.

clauses.label: Section 14.
clauses.text:
Section 14. Steamers actually carrying fifty or more through passengers
will be given preference over other vessels in transiting. 'To avail themselves
of this privilege, such vessels, however, must report by radio the number of
such passengers on board.

clauses.label: Section 15.
clauses.text:
Section 15. The Canal authorities may hold a vessel for the purpose of
investigating any report made against her by the proper persons, for the viola-
tion of the rules of the Canal or the laws of the Canal Zone, or of the United
States, or for the investigation or adjustment of any claims or disputes that
may arise on either side; but no vessel shall have any claim for damages against
the Canal for any delay in consequence thereof.

clauses.label: Section 16.
clauses.text:
Section 16. Unauthorized possession or transportation of intoxicating liquors
in the Canal Zone is a violation of Title III, Section 20, of the U. S. National
Prohibition Act. The transportation of intoxicating liquors in transit by vessels
is not prohibited. Liquors for medical stores may be procured by application
to the Chief Health Officer, and orders for liquors for ships' stores for foreign
vessels and for American passenger vessels for use outside of the Canal Zone
must bc approved by the Chief Customs Inspector.
PILOTS ANI) MOVEMENTS OF VESSELS.

clauses.label: Section 17.
clauses.text:
Section 17. Except when exempted in each case by the Governor of The
Panama Canal, no vessel will be allowed to pass through the Canal, enter or
leave a terminal port, maneuver, shift berth, go alongside or leave any wharf
or dock in Canal waters without having a regularly authorized Government
pilot on board and specific authority from the Port Captain. The fact that the
master or anY officer of any vessel holds a pilot's license for any of the waters
of the Canal Zone will not authorize the vessel to enter or move without taking
a Government pilot. No vessel in danger or distress will be prohibited from
entering a terminal port at any time in case of necessity or emergency; but
such vessel should, when practicable, give due notice in advance, by radio or
otherwise, and obtain a pilot, if possible; nor shall this be interpreted to prevent
a vessel from anchoring in the anchorage described in Article 2 -.

clauses.label: Section 18.
clauses.text:
Section 18. Whenever in the judgment of the Receiving and Forwarding
Agent, or Port Captain, it is dleemned advisable to shift any vessel not fully
2

engaged in receiving or discharging cargo, in order to accommodate other ves-
sels, or for any other reason, shifting will be made by direction of the Port
Captain, and the towing and other expenses thereby incurred will be charged
against the vessel so shifted. No vessel at any dock or moorings within the
Panama Canal shall disable her engines or otherwise be rendered inoperative
except on specific authority from the Port Captain concerned.

clauses.label: Section 19.
clauses.text:
Section 19. Pilotage for vessels in transit through the Canal is free, but
should any vessel, while in Canal waters, discharge or receive freight or pas-
sengers, or take on hoard supplies, provisions, stores, or fuel, or remain for the
purp. ce of effecting repairs or make either terminal a port of call, she is liable
for entrance and/or departure pilotage.

clauses.label: Section 20.
clauses.text:
Section 20. No person, steamer, company or corporation v~ ill be allowed to
maintain or employ pilots in Canal waters for the exclusive use of their own or
any other vessels.

clauses.label: Section 2r.
clauses.text:
Section 2r. If a vessel is not boarded immediately on arrival she may anchor
and await the boarding party. Vessels anchoring at the Pacific entrance will
do o in an area bounded by San Jose Rock, Flamenco Island, channel buoys
Nos. 4 and 2, and at the Atlantic entrance just inside the West breakwater.
Should a vessel desire a pilot to meet her outside of the Atlan~tic breakwaters,
she should remain there and make signal to that effect.

clauses.label: Section 22.
clauses.text:
Section 22. All vessels entering port must tare the berth or docks assigned
them by the Port Captain.

clauses.label: Section 23.
clauses.text:
Section 23. No vessel will be allowed to anchor in any part of the Canal,
except in an emergency. Vessels may be permitted by the Port Captain to
anchor in Gatun Lake, in suitable localities outside the prism limits, or to moor
to the approach walls of the locks, or in established mooring stations.

clauses.label: Section 24.
clauses.text:
Section 24. The captain or master of a vessel in Canal waters, except while
the vessel is being passed through the locks, shall be charged with the safe
handling and proper navigation of the vessel; the pilot is to be considered as
being on board solely in an advisory capacity, but masters of vessels must abide
by the rules and regulations of the Canal, as interpreted by the pilot.

clauses.label: Section 25.
clauses.text:
Section 25. The Panama Canal assumes responsibility for the safe handling
of a vessel in the locks from the time the first towing wire is made fast on board,
on entering, until all towing wires are cast off, on leaving. This holds good,
however, only in cases where the vessel has complied with all the requirements
of these regulations, and where motive power, steering gear, and other appur-
tenances for controlling the ship function properly.

clauses.label: Section 26.
clauses.text:
Section 26. The, pilot shall be consulted freely at all times to insure safety
in navigation, and that no accident or damage result from ignorance on the part
of the master or officers of the vessel in transit; and should any such master,
officer or persons connected with the ship, give or cause to be given, any order,
or direct any change of speed or direction of the ship on his own initiative, with-
out the knowledge of the pilot or against his advice, which may result in dardiage
to his own or any other vessel or Canal property of any kind, or endanger or block
the Canal, he will be held -rictly responsible, and the vessel itself may be held
by legal process until settlement in full shall have been made to cover any loss
or damage that may have resulted in consequence thereof.

clauses.label: Section 27.
clauses.text:
Section 27. When, in the opinion of the pilot, the master or captain or his
representatives have failed to follow the pilot's advice and thereby endangered
his own or any other vessel or any part of the Canal or its equipment, the pilot
shall then direct the master or captain of such vessel to stop, anchor, or moor,
until the fact-- have been laid before the Canal authorities.

clauses.label: Section 28.
clauses.text:
Section 28. Inasmuch as every, vessel has its own individual peculiarities
representative, to be present at all times on the bridge of the ship to keep the
pilot informed in regard to these matters, so that the pilot may be best qualified
give advice in regard to safely navigating the ship.

clauses.label: Section 29.
clauses.text:
Section 29. The pilot shall inform the master or captain that his experience
and knowledge of the Canal is at the latter's disposal and that inasmuch as the
3

pilot is not in a position to know the defects, difficulties, or eccentric ,ies of the
vessel in maneuvering, while getting under way or in transit, the responsibility
for navigating the vessel is entirely in the hands of the master or captain, except
when passing through the locks.
3. PREPARATION FOR AND TRANSIT THROUGH THE CANAL.

clauses.label: Section 30.
clauses.text:
Section 30. Incoming ships will be boarded inside the Atlantic breakwater
or off the seaward end of dredged channel at the Pacific entrance by a boarding
party, which consists, in addition to the pilot, of the quarantine officer (immi-
gration), boarding officer (customs), admeasurer, and commissary representative.
Ships arriving between sunrise and 10 p. mn. will be boarded on arrival. Those
arriving after io p. mn. will be boarded at sunrise. Vessels boarded between sun-
set and 10 p. in. will be suailed to a charge (passenger vessels, $40; others $20)
