clauses.text:
1. Classifcation.-The consular branch of the Foreign Service of the United
States consists, first, of Foreign Service officers duly appointed by the President and
assigned to duty as consuls general, Foreign Service inspectors, consuls, vice consuls,
and student interpreters. These are known as "career officers". Secondly, there
are non-career officers, commissioned or appointed by the Secretary of State, viz.,
vice consuls who are not Foreign Service officers, consular agents, and clerks at
consulates.

2. Definitions.-" Foreign Service officer" shall be deemed to denote permanent
officers in the Foreign Service below the grade of minister.-Act of May 24, 1924,

clauses.label: Sec. 2.
clauses.text:
Sec. 2.
"Consular officer" shall be deemed to include consuls general, consuls, vice
consuls, student interpreters, and consular agents and none others.-R. S. 1674, as
amended, 38 Stat. L. 806.
" Consul general" and "consul" shall be deemed to denote full, principal and
permanent consular officers as distinguished from subordinates and substitutes.-
R. S. 1674, as amended, 38 ,Stat. L. 806.
The term "consul", whenever the sense so requires, denotes any principal
consular officer or any person invested by the United States with, and exercising,
the functions of consul general, consul or vice consul.-R. S. 4130, as amended,
19 Stat. L. 2. As ordinarily used, in a specific sense, it denotes a particular grade of
consular officer, but it is sometimes used, in a generic sense, to embrace all consular
officers.-15 C. Mu. R?. 74.
The term "vice consul" denotes any officer holding a commission as vice consul,
whether he be a Foreign Service officer or not.-R. 5. 1674, as amended, 8 Stat. L.

806.
The term "substitute consular officers" denotes vice consuls when in responsible
charge of a consulate general or consulate.-R. 5. 1674, as amended, 88 Stat. L. 806.
The term "subordinate consular officers" denotes vi .e consuls when not in
charge of consulates general or consulates, student interpreters and consular agents.
-R. S. 1674, as amended, 38 Stat. L. 806.

3. Entry into the Foreign Servie.Appointments to the position of Foreign
Service officer are made aft examination and a, period of probation of one year
in an unclassified grade or, after five years of continuous service in the Depart-
ment of State, by transfer therefrom to any class in the Foreign Service upon the
recommendation of the Foreign Service Personnel Board and with the approval
of the Secretary of State.-Act of May 24, 1924, See. 5; E. 0. June 7, 1924, Sec.
o3(b). An accurate record of the efficiency of all officers and employees of the
Department of State is kept for this purpose.--38 Stat. L. 806, as amended, Act
of May 24, 1924, Sec. 6. Reinstatement of Foreign Service officers separated from
the classified service by reason of appointment to some other position in the Gov-
ernment service may be made by Executive order of the President under such rules
and regulations as he may prescribe. Act of May 24, 1924, Sec. 5.
All appointments of Foreign Service officers are by commission to a class and
not by commission to any particular post, and such officers are assigned to posts
and may be transferred from one post to another by order of the President as the
interests of the Service may require.-Act of May 24, 1924, Sec. 5.
New appointments to the Service are made to the grade of Foreign Service
officer, unclassified. The names of candidates eligible for appointment after
examination remain on an eligible list for two years except in the case of those
candidates who within that period are appointed or who withdraw their names.
Names which have been on the eligible list for two years are dropped therefrom
and the candidates concerned are not again eligible for appointment unless upon

2
fresh application, designation anew for examination, and the successful passing of
such examination.-Act of May 24, 1924, See. 5; E. 0. June 7, 1924, Sec. 2, 19.

4. Examination for the Foreign Service.-(a) Examinations to determine the
eligibility of candidates for the Foreign Service are held by a Board of Examiners
composed as follows: The Undersecretary of State, two Assistant Secretaries of
State to be designated by the Secretary of State, the Chairman of the Executive
Committee of the Foreign Service Personnel Board, and the Chief Examiner of
the Civil Service Commission or such person as may be designated by him to
serve in his stead.

clauses.label: (b)
clauses.text:
(b) It is the duty of the Board of Examiners to formulate rules for and hold
examinations of applicants for commission to the Foreign Service and to determine
from among the persons designated by the President for examination those who are
fitted for appointment.

clauses.label: (c)
clauses.text:
(c) The scope and method of the examinations is determined by the Board of
Examiners, but among the subjects are included the -'allowing: at least one modern
language other than English (French, Spanish, or German-by preference), elements
of international law, geography, the natural, industrial, and commercial resources
and the commerce of the United States; American history, government and insti-
tutions; the history since 1850 of Europe, Latin America and the Far East, elements
of political economy, commercial and maritime law.

clauses.label: (d)
clauses.text: (d) The examinations are both written and oral.

clauses.label: (e)
clauses.text:
(e) Examinations are rated on a scale of 100, and no person rated at less than
80 is eligible for certification.

clauses.label: (f)
clauses.text:
(f) No one is certified as eligible who is under twenty-one or over thirty-five
years of age, or who is not a citizen of the United States, or who is not of good
character and habits and physically, mentally, and temperamentally qualified for
the proper performance of the duties of the Foreign Service, or who has not been
specially designated by the President for appointment subject to examination and
to the occurrence of an appropriate vacancy.

clauses.label: (g)
clauses.text:
(g) Upon the conclusion of the examinations, the names of the candidates who
have attained upon the whole examination the required rating are certified by the
Board to the Secretary of State as eligible for appointment.-E. 0. June 7, 1924,
Sec. 12-18.

clauses.label: (h)
clauses.text:
(h) The Secretary of State reports to the President along with his recommen-
dations the names of persons found upon taking the prescribed examination to have
fitness for appointment to the lower grades of the service.-88 Stat. L. 806, as
amended, Act of May 24, 1924, Sec. 6.

clauses.label: (i)
clauses.text:
(i) Applicants for appointment who are designated to take an examination and
who fail to report therefor, are not entitled to take a subsequent examination unless
they are specifically designated to take such subsequent examination.

clauses.label: (j)
clauses.text:
(j) In designations for appointment subject to examinatioh and in appoint-
ments after examination, due regard is had to the principle that as between candi-
dates of equal merit, appointments should be made so as to tend to secure propor-
tional representation of all the States and Territories in the Foreign Service; and
neither in the designation for examination nor certification nor appointment after
examination are the political affiliations of the candidates considered.

clauses.label: (k)
clauses.text:
(k) The Board of Examiners issues notices and, makes rules for accomplishing
the objects of the foregoing regulations.-E. 0. June 7, 1924, Sec. 20-2f2.

5. Classes and salaries in the Foreign Service.-The officers in the Foreign
Service are graded and classified with the salaries of each class, as follows, but
not exceeding in number for each class a proportion to the total number of officers
in the Service represented in the following percentage limitations:
Ambassador,
Minister, provided by law.
Class 1, 6 per centutm, $9,000.
Class 2, 7 per centum, $8,000.
Class 3, 8 per centum, $7,000.
Class 4, 9 per centum, $6,000.
Class 5, 10 per centum, $5,000.
Class 6, 14 per centum, $4,500.
Class 7,------$4,000.
Class 8,-------$3,500.
Class 9,----- $3,000.
Unclassified-----$3,000. to $1,500.
--Act of May 24, 1924, Section 8.

3

6. Promotion in the Serv~ice and separation from the Service.-AII Foreign Service
officers are subject to promotion on merit.-Act of May 24, 1924, Sec. R. Vacancies
in all classes from 1 to 9 are filled by promotion from lower classes, based upon
ability and efficiency as shown in the Service. The Foreign Service Personnel
Board submits to the Secretary of State lists of those Foreign Service officers whose
records of efficiency entitle them to advancement in the Service, and who are
therefore recommended for promotion. All action taken by the Board is strictly
non-partisan, and based exclusively upon the record of efficiency of the officers
concerned.-E. 0. June 7, 1924, See. 1, 5(b), 8.
The Secretary of State reports from time to time to the President, along
with his recommendations, the names of those Foreign Service officers who by
reason of efficient service have demonstrated special efficiency.-Act of May 24,
1924, Sec. 6. No promotions from the unclassified grade to higher grades are
made except on the recommendations of the Foreign Service Personnel Board,
with the approval of the Secretary of State, after the completion of one full term
of instruction, or the equivalent thereof in the Foreign Service School.-E. 0.
June 7, 1924, Sec. 23. Upon recommendation by the Foreign Service Personnel
Board the Secretary of State reports to the President, along with his recommenda-
tions, the names of those Foreign Service officers who by reason of efficient service
have demonstrated special capacity for promotion to the grade of minister. The
lists thus submitted enumerate the names of the officers in the order of merit,
each such list being complete in itself, superseding all previous lists. A list is
submitted to the Secretary of State whenever there is a vacancy in the grade of
minister or when requested by the President or the Secretary of State and in no
case does it contain more names than there are vacancies to fill. Each 'list is
signed by the Chairman and at least three members of the Board, and if approved
by the Secretary of State, is submitted to the President.-Act of May 24, 1924x,
Sec. 6; E. 0. June 7, 1924, Sec. 5 (c).
The Foreign Service Personnel Board submits to the Secretary of State the
names of those Foreign Service officers who are recommended for designation as
counselors of embassy or legation.-E. 0. June 7, 1924, Sec. 5 (d).
Separation from the Service. Whenever it is determined that the efficiency
" rating of an officer is poor and below the required standard for the Service, the
Personnel Board so notifies the officer, and if after due notification the rating of
such officer continues nevertheless to be unsatisfactory, his name is reported to
the Secretary of State with a full recital of the circumstances and a recommenda-
tion of the Board for separation from the Service. Whenever such recommenda-
tion for separation from the Service is made, the Board at the same time notifies
the officer of the action taken.-E. 0. June 7, 1924, Sec. 6.

7. Foreigi Service Personnel Board.-The Foreign Service Personnel Board is
composed as follows: The Undersecretary of State who is the Chairman, two
Assistant Secretaries of State designated by the Secretary of State, and the members
of the Executive Committee of the Foreign Service Personnel Board.
Duties of th~e Board. (a) To examine into the character, ability, efficiency,
experience and general availability of all Foreign Service officers and to submit to
the Secretary of State such information as he may require regarding the efficiency
records of such officers.

clauses.label: (b)
clauses.text:
(b) From time to time, as vacancies arise, to submit to the Secretary of State
lists of those Foreign Service officers whose records of efficiency entitle them to
advancement in the Service, and who are therefore recommended for promotion,
and the names of those officers and employees in the Department of State who,
after five years of continuous service, and because of special ability and merit
are recommended for appointment by transfer to the position of Foreign Service
officer. All such lists are signed by the Chairman and at least three members of
the Board, except in the case of a tie vote when the Secretary of State decides.

clauses.label: (c)
clauses.text:
(c) To submit to the Secretary of State the names of those Foreign Service
officers who, in the opinion of the Board, have demonstrated special capacity for
promotion to the grade of minister. Each list thus submitted enumerates the
names of the officers in the order of merit and is complete in itself, superseding all
previous lists. A list is submitted to the Secretary of State whenever there is a
vacancy in the grade of minister or when requested by the President or the Secre-
tary of State and in no case does it contain more names than there are vacancies
to fill. Each such list is signed by the Chairman and at least three members of the
Board, and if approved by the Secretary of State, is submitted to the President.

4

clauses.label: (d)
clauses.text:
(d) To submit to the Secretary of State the names of those Foreign Service
officers who are recommended for designation as counselors of embassy or legation.

clauses.label: (e)
clauses.text:
(e) To recommend to the Secretary of State the assignment of Foreign Service
officers to posts and the transfer of such officers from one branch of the Service to
the other according to the needs of the Service.

clauses.label: (f)
clauses.text:
(f) To consider controversies and delinquencies among the service personnel
and recommend to the Secretary appropriate disciplinary measures where required.

clauses.label: (g)
clauses.text:
(g) For the purposes stated in paragraphs (e) and (f), the Undersecretary of
State, and two Assistant Secretaries of State who are members of the Board are
deemed to constitute the full Poard, but the Executive Committee has the power of
recommendation.
Proceedings of thes Board. The members of the Board, individually and col-
lectively, have authority to examine all records and data relating to the personnel
of the S -rvice.
All action taken by the Board is strictly non-partisan, and based exclusively
upon the record of efficiency of the officers concerned.
The proceedings of the Board are strictly confidential, but the Chairman may,
and it is a part of his duty, within a reasonable time prior to each meeting of the
Board for recommending promotions, demotions or removals, to invite the Chairman
of the Senate Committee on Foreign Relations and the Chairman of the House
Committee on Foreign Affairs or some Committee member designated by the Chair-
man, to sit with the Board through its deliberations without, however, participating
in its decisions.
The Board elects its secretary from among its members.
The Executive Committee of the Foreign Service Personnel Board is com-
posed of a Chairman, and two Foreign Service officers of high rank representing
both the diplomatic and the consular branches of the Foreign Service, selected by
the other members of the Personnel Board with the approval of the Secretary of
State.
The Secretary of State prescribes the duties of the Executive Committee.-
E. 0. June 7, 1924, Sec. 4-11.

8. Efficiency records of Foreign Service officer.-The Department of State
keeps a permanent efficiency record for Foreign Service officers of all grades cover-
ing each officer's fitness for the Service as shown by his ability, promptness and
diligence in performing the duties of his office; his general conduct in office; and
the character of the reports which he makes.-88 Stat. L. 806, as amended, Act of
May 24, 1924, Sec. 6.

9. The Foreign Service School-There is established in the Department of
State a FrinService School for the instruction of new appointees.
The oreign_ Service School is under the direction of a Foreign Service School
Board, composed of the following members: the Undersecretary of State, two
Assistant Secretaries of State designated by the Secretary of State, the Chairman
of the Executive Committee of the Foreign Service Personnel Board, and the
Chief Instructor of the Foreign Service School. The School Board acts in all
matters with the approval of the Secretary of State.
The Chief Instructor is selected by the other members of the School Board
from among the officers of the Foreign Service, with the approval of the Secretary
of State.
Other instructors are selected from among the qualified officers of the Depart-
ment of State, the Foreign Service, the other executive departments of the Govern-
ment, and other available sources in the discretion of the School Board.
The term of instruction in the Foreign Service School is one year which is con-
sidered a period of probation during which the new appointees are judged as to
their qualifications for advancement and assignment to duty. At the end of the
term, recommendations are made to the Secretary of State by the Personnel Board
for the dismissal of any who have failed to meet the re..red standard of the
Service.
The Secretary of State prescribes rules and regulations for the governance of
the Foreign Service School.-E. 0. June 7, 1924, Sec. 25-80.

10. Appointments of secretaries in the diplomatic service and cones~r oficer.--
The President nominates, and by and with the advice and consent of the Senate,
appoints secretaries in the diplomatic service, consuls general, consuls, vice consuls
of career, and student interpreters.-- U. S. Constitution, Art. 1, Sec. 9. Vice consuls

U
5
not of career and consular agents are appointed by the Secretary of State.-R. S.

1695.
Foreign Service officers may be appointed as secretaries in the diplomatic ser-
vice or as consular officers, or both, but all such appointments are made by and with
the advice and consent of the Senate.-Act of May 24, 1924, Sec. 4.

11. Assignment to duty of Foreign Service offiers.-Foreign Service officers may
be assigned to duty in either the diplomatic or the consular branch of the Foreign
Service at the discretion of the President.-Act of May 24, 1924, Sec. 4.
The President may, whenever he considers it advisable so to do, designate and
assign any Foreign Service officer as counselor of embassy or legation.-Act of May
24, 1924, Sec. 16.
Any Foreign Service officer may, within the discretion of the President, be
appointed to act as commissioner, charg6 d'affaires, minister resident or diplomatic
agent, for such period as the public interests may require, without loss of grade,
class, or salary, provided, however, that no such officer shall receive more than one
salary..-Act of .May .94, 1924, Sec. 17.
Any Foreign Service officer may be assigned for duty in the~ Department of
State without loss of class or salary, such assignment to be for a period of not more
than three years, unless the public interests demand further service, when such
assignment may be extended for a period not to exceed one year. Foreign Service
officers may also be detailed for special duty not at their posts nor in the Depart-
ment of State, but such special duty shall not continue for more than sixty days
unless in the case of trade conferences or international gatherings, congresses or
conferences.-Act of May 24, 1924, Sec. 14.

12. Oficial acts of Foreign Service oficers.-All official acts of Foreign Service
officers while on duty in either the diplomatic or the consular branch of the Foreign
Service shall be performed under their respective commissions as secretaries or as
consular officers.-Act of May 24, 1924, Sec. 4.

13. Oath of ogfice.-Whenever any person is appointed to any office of honor
or trust under the Government of the United States he shall, before entering upon
the duties of his office, take and subscribe the following oath: "I, A. B., do solemnly
swear (or affirm) that I will support and defend the Constitution of the United States
against all enemies, foreign and domestic; that I will bear true faith and allegiance
to the same; that I take this obligation freely, without any mental reservation or
purpose of evasion; and that I will well and faithfully discharge the duties of the
office on which I am about to enter. So help me God."-R. S. 1757.
The foregoing requirement applies to all Foreign Service officers, secretaries
in the diplomatic service, consuls general, consuls, vice consuls, student interpreters,
and if citizens of the United States, to consular agents.
The oath of office may be taken before any officer who is authorized either
by the laws of the United States, or by the local municipal law, to administer
oaths, in the State, Territory, or District where such oath may be administered.-R.
S. 1758. The oath may not, however, be taken abroad except before some officer
of the United States authorized to administer oaths.

14. Bonds of Foreign Service officers, secretaries in the diplomatic service, con-
suls general, consuls, and 'vice consuls of career, and others.-Every secretary, consul
general, consul, vice consul of career, or Foreign Service officer, before he receives
his commission or enters upon the duties of his office, shall give to the United
States a bond, in such form as the President shall prescribe, with such sureties,
who shall be permanent residents of the United States, as the Secretary of State
shall approve, in a penal sum not less than the annual compensation allowed to
such officer, conditioned for the true and faithful accounting for, paying over and
delivering up of all fees, moneys, goods, effects, books, records, papers, and other
property which shall come to his hands or to the hands of any other person to his
use as such officer under any law now or hereafter enacted, and for the true and
faithful perfomance of all other duties now or hereafter lawfully imposed upon
him as such officer. Such bond shall cover by its stipulations all official acts of
such officer, whether as Foreign Service officer, or as secretary in the diplomatic
service, consul general, consul, or vice consul of career.-Act of May 24, 1924,

clauses.label: Sec. 9.
clauses.text:
Sec. 9.
Bands of vice consuls not of career. Vice consuls not of career shall give bond,
with such sureties and stipulations as the Secretary of State may direct.
Bonds of consular agents. No bond is required of consular agents, but a con-

6
sular officer having an agent under his supervision, may take from him such bond
as the officer may deem proper to protect himself.

15. Custody, withdrawal and cancellation of bonds, and sureties on bonds.-The
bonds of officers in the consular branch of the Foreign Service, after their approval
by the Secretary of State, are deposited with the Secretary of the Treasury.-Act
of May 24, 1904, Sec. 9.
Withdrawal and cancellation of bonds. Under the rule of the Treasury Depart-
ment, bends, when filed with it, can not be withdrawn from its custody; and they
are not canceled on the retirement of the officer from the Service.
Sureties on bonds. The sureties on bonds of salaried officers shall be permanent
residents of the United States or a regularly authorized surety company incor-
porated under the laws of the United States or of one of the States, and must be
approved by the Secretary of State.-28 Stat. L. 279. Married women will not be
accepted as sureties.-15 Op. Att. Gen. 472.

16. Foreign Service inspectors.-The provisions of section 4 of the Act of April
5, 1906, relative to the powers, duties and prerogatives of consuls general at large
are applicable to Foreign Service officers detailed for the purposes of inspection,
who, under the direction of the Secretary of State, inspect the work of offices in
the Foreign Service, both in the diplomatic and the consular branches.-Act of May
24, 1924x, Sec. 10.
Each consular office shall be inspected at least once in every two years. When-
ever the President has reason to believe that the business of a consulate or a con-
sulate general is not being properly conducted and that it is necessary for the public
interest, he may authorize any inspector to suspend the consul or consul general,
and administer the office in his stead for a period of not exceeding ninety days.
In such case the inspector so authorized shall have power to suspend any vice
consular officer or clerk in said office during the period aforesaid.-34 Stat. L. 100.
The suggestions and directions given by a Foreign Service inspector at the
time of any inspection of an office must be implicitly followed and obeyed, in the
absence of contrary instructions from the Department of State. The principal
officer will insure that the consular agents under his supervision comply with the
inspector's directions left with them. He will also bring the inspector's directions
to the attention of his successor in office.
An officer, upon assuming charge of an office, will accept the suggestions and
instructions left for his predecessor as applicable to himself and to his own adminis-
tration of the office.

17. Vice consul8.-There are twvo categories of vice consuls, those of career
and those who are not of career. The former are Foreign Service officers com-
missioned as vice consuls; the latter are commissioned by the Secretary of State as
occasion may require, usually from among the clerks at consular offices.
Duties of -vice consuls. All vice consuls are consular officers subordinate to
principal consular officers (consuls general and consuls), exercising and performing
the duties within the limits of their consulates at the same or at different points
and places from those at which the principals are located.-R. S. 1674; 38 Stat.
L. 806; 33 Fed. Rep. 167.
Vice consuls, whether of career or not, perform such duties of the consular
offices to which- they may be assigned as are described in the Consular Regulations
and Laws of the United States, and which they may be directed to perform by the
principal officer under whom they serve. When the principal officer is absent, the
ranking consular officer, or, if there be two of equal grade, the one whose commis-
sion bears the earlier date, in the absence of contrary instructions from the Depart-
ment of State, will assume full charge of the office under his bond.
1S. Vice consuls not of career.-Vice consuls not of career are not eligible to
advancement in the Service without undergoing examination and qualifying for
appointment as Foreign Service officers. They are appointed to particular posts,
and receive certificates of appointment to those posts, which are forwarded to them
through the appropriate diplomatic missions.
Citizenship. Every vice consul must be an American citizen.-40 Stat. L. 1333.
Removal of vice consuls. Consuls general and consuls have no power to remove
vice consuls assigned to their offices or to ;service under their supervision. In cases
of serious insubordination, threatened destruction or loss of government property,
or conduct likely to injure the reputation of the consulate, the principal consular
officer may suspend the vice consul responsible therefor from office pending a review
11

7
of the facts by the Secretary of State. The Secretary of State will invariably be
notified by telegraph of a suspension. A report of the facts, accompanied by a
signed statement of the vice consul in his own behalf, will be forwarded by the
most expeditious method. While under suspension a vice consul may not perform
any official act.

19. Student interpreters.-Student interpreters are Foreign Service officers,
unclassified, who are appointed by the President by and with the advice and con-
sent of the Senate and assigned to posts, generally in oriental countries, for the
purpose of studying and perfecting themselves in the languages' Zf such countries.
After acquiring a knowledge of the language of the country and passing the
first examination for promotion, usually at the end of the second year of service,
student interpreters are advanced to the grade of vice consul. After passing the
second examination, usually at the end of the third or fourth year, they are ad-
vanced to a higher salary class. They are thereafter eligible for advancement in
the Service without further examination, on the basis of demonstrated ability and
efficiency.

20. Consular Agents.-Consular agents are appointed by the Secretary of State,
usually upon the nomination of the principal consular officer.-R. S. 1696. The
practice of making such nominations must not be construed to limit the authority
of the Secretary of State to appoint these officers without such previous nomination
by the principal officer.
The term "Consular agents" denotes consular officers subordinate to principal
officers exercising the powers vested in them and performing the duties prescribed
for them by regulation of the President, at posts or places different from those at
which such principals are located.-R. S. 1674, as amended, 88 Stat. L. 806. Their
functions are not, in all respects, as extensive as those of the principal officer.
Though they act at places different; from the seat of the principal office and their
duties are in substance the same toward persons desiring consular services, they act
only as the representative of the principal, and are subject and subordinate to him.
They are not authorized to correspond with the Department of State, unless through
the principal or under exceptional circumstances; they make no returns or reports
directly to the Department, and they are not permitted to render accounts or make
any drafts for expenditures on the departments of the Government unless under
express instructions.
Consular agents are subject, like other consular officers, to the provisions cf
law and the instructions of the Department of State. As soon as a consular agent
has entered upon his duties, a specimen of his signature and an impression of his
official seal should be sent to the Department.
Citizenship of consular agents. In all cases, where it is practicable, consular
agents should be citizens of the United States, and none other should be recom-
mended for appointment, unless citizens of proper character and standing can not
be found.
Acting consular agents. No consular agent has authority to appoint a sub-
agent. In case of emergency, or in the absence of the consular agent on leave, the
principal consular officer may designate, with the approval of the Department of
State, a suitable person to perform the duties under the title of Acting Consular
Agent. The principal consular officer should, at the time the change is made,
report to the Department the name of the person whom he has designated as Acting
Consular Agent during the temporary absence of the agent from his post, and
accompany the report with the signature of the substitute and an impression of the
official seal of the agency.
A person placed temporarily in charge of a consular agency should sign as
Acting Consular Agent. Acting consular agents must not perform notarial acts.

21. Clerks at consulates.-Clerks at consulates are, so far as practicable,
appointed under Civil Service rules and regulations.-42 Stat. L. 602. In practice
they are frequently nominated by the consuls but their appointment is subject to
approval by the Secretary of State and the Department reserves the right to fill
such clerkships directly by appointment from the Unlted States or from American
citizens abroad. In nominating persons for clerkships consuls must give the
qualifications of the nominees in the form prescribed by the Department together
with the proposed amount of compensation of each clerk ai~d the allowance from
which paid. No clerk shall receive increased compensation without the authority
of the Secretary of State.

FM
(Ntizensh~ip of clerks. Preference shall be given to American citizens in nomi-
nations for clerkships whenever properly qualified persons can be found.
No person who is not an American citizen shall be appointed at any consulate
general or consulate to any clerical position the salary of which is $1,000 or more.--
34 Stat. L. 101.
Members of coatsular ojficer's family. The appointment " _ mbers of a con-
sular officer's family will be permitted only in exceptional cases wt . t1 a expediency
of such an appointment and the qualifications of the applicant arc clearly shown.
In no case does the Department permit the ap'pointmc it of the'fe male members
of the consular officer's family as clerks in his office.
CManges in clerical personnel. Consular officers must report promnptly. to the
Department every change in the clerical personnel of their offices.
Eficiency reports and records. The Department maintains a system of efficiency
reports and records applying to clerks, messengers and other non-career subordinates
including consular agents. These records are consulted in connection with transfers
and increases in compensation.
Coi/dential nature of reports and recommendations. The efficiency records
of clerks and other subordinates are strictly confidential and no efficiency report
or rating is to be divulged by any consular officer except to Foreign Service Inspectors
and supervising consuls general. All recommendations for increases in compensa-
tion for clerks or other subordinates are to be held confidential and in no instance
disclosed to the persons concerned. Recommendations for the commissioning of
clerks as vice consuls shall be treated in a like manner.
Clerks commiss-ioned as vice consuls. A clerk at a consulate will be commissioned
as vice consul only when conditions at the post make an additional signing officer
necessary.

22. Prohibition against engaging in business.-No consular officer whose salary
exceeds one thousand dollars a year, shall, while he holds his office, be interested
in or transact any business as a merchant, factor, broker or other trader, or as a
clerk or other agent for any such person to, from, or within the port, place, or limits
of his jurisdiction, directly or indirectly, either in his own name or in the name or
through the agency of any other person; nor shall he practice as a lawyer for com-pensation or be interested in the fees or compensation of any lawyer; and he shall
in his official bond stipulate as a condition thereof not to violate this prohibition.-
R. S. 16,99, 1700; 34 Stat. L. 101.
No consular officer whose salary exceeds $1,000. per annum shall make any
investments of money within the limits of the country from the government of
which he has received his recognition or exequatur. This prohibition applies to
the owning of real estate, or of bonds, shares, stocks, mortgages, etc. There is no
objection to a consular officer's depositing money in a bank which happens to give
interest on current ace -iunts or fixed deposits; and a consular officer may buy a
house and land for his own use, but he may not do so as an investment or speculation.

23. Jurisdiction of consuls general.-All consuls general are charged with the
ordinary duties of a consul within the prescribed limits of their respective districts.

24. Limits of consular districts.-The statute authorizes the President to define
the extent of country to be embraced within any consulate.-R?. S. 1696. The
consular commission usually describes these limits as including all places nearer
to the official residence of a consul than to the '*esidence of any other consul within
the same allegiance. This is to be regarded as the rule by which the limits of the
respective districts are to be determined in the absence of instructions specifically
defining the consular district. In no case, however, is a consular officer authorized
to takes jurisdiction of consular business outside of the state from the government
of which he receives his exequatur. The Department of State may, however, .nits discretion, assign a consular agency to a consulate without regard to nearnessof geographical situation. The limits of a consular agency are always within thedistrict of the consulate to which it is attached, unless the Department shall
deternune otherwise.

when they are designated for service as diplomatic or as consular officers. All

provisions of law, however, which are inconsistent with the act of May 24, 1924,

ARTICLE II -q Y'" v
RETIREMENT OF FOREIGN SERVICE OFFICERS

31. Retirement of Foreign Service officers provided by law.--The law provides
for the retirement of Foreign Service officers on account of age or disability and
authorize the President to prescribe rules and regulations to give effect to the
statute. The administration of the retirement system is placed under the direc-
tion of the Secretary of State.-Act of May 24, 1924, Sec. 18.

32. Retirement on account of age.-When any Foreign Service officer has reached
the age of sixty-five years and rendered at least fifteen years of service he is retired,
but the President may in his discretion retain any such officer on active duty for
such period no~t exceeding five years as he may deem for the interest of the United
States--Act of May 24, 1924,, Sec. 18 (d).

33. Retirement on account of disability.-Any Foreign Service officer who before
reaching the age of retirement becomes totally disabled for useful and efficient
service' by reason of disease or injury not due to vicious habits, intemperance, or
willful misconduct on his part, is, upon his own application or upon order of the
President, retired on an annuity. In each case such disability is determined by
the report of a duly qualified physician or surgeon designated by the Secretary of
State -to conduct the examination. Unless the disability be permanent, a like exam-
ination is made annually in order to determine the degree of disability, and the
payment of annuity ceases from the date of the medical examination showing
recovery.
Fees for examinations under this provision, together with reasonable traveling
and other expenses incurred in order to submit to examination, are paid out of the
Foreign Service Retirement and Disability Fund.--Act of May 24,1924, Sec. 18 (j).

34. Ambassadors, ministers, and persons appointed to the Department.-Any
diplomatic secretary or consular officer who prior to July 1, 1924, was, or any
Foreign Service officer who subsequent to July 1, 1924, may be, promoted from
the classified service to the grade of ambassador or minister, or appointed to a
position in the Department of State is entitled to all the benefits of retirement in
the same manner and under the same conditions as Foreign Service officers.-
Act of May 24y, 1924, Sec. 18 (o).

35. Period of service.-The period of service is computed from the date of
original oath of office as secretary in the diplomatic service, consul general, consul,
vice consul, deputy consul, consular assistant, consular agent, commercial agent,
interpreter, or student interpreter, and includes periods of service at different
times in either the diplomatic or consular service, or while on assignment to the
Department of State, or on special duty, but all periods of separation from the
service and so much of any period of leave of absence as may exceed six months
are excluded. Service in the Department of State prior to appointment as a Foreign
Service officer may be included in the period of service under certain conditions.--
Act of May 240, 1924, Sec. 18 (p).
The President has the authority to establish by Executive order, a list of places
in tropical countries which by reason of climatic or other extreme conditions are
to be classed is unhealthful posts, and each year of duty at such posts, while so
cla,,,,d, inclusive of regular leaves of absence, shall be counted as one year and a
half, and so on in like proportion in reckoning the length of service for the purposes
of retirement.-Act of May 24, 1924, Sec. 18 (k,).

36. Foreign Service Retirement and Disability Fund.-Five per centum of the
basic salary of all Foreign Service officers eligible to retirement is contributed to
the Foreign Service Retirement and Disability Fund and the Secretary of the
Treasury causes such deductions to be made and the sums to be transferred on
the books of the Treasury Department to the credit of the Foreign Service Retire-
ment and Disability Fund for the payment of annuities, refunds, and allowances,
provided that all basic salaries in excess of $9,000. per annum are treated as $9,000.-
Act of May 24, 1924x, Sec. 18 (c).

10
In case service in the Department of State prior to appointment as a Foreign
Service officer is included in the period of service, the officer shall pay into the
Foreign Service Retirement and Disability Fund a special contribution equal to
5 per centum of his annual salary for each year of such employment, with interest
thereon to the date of payment compounded annually at 4 per centum.-Act of
May 24, 1924, Sec. 18 (p).
The Secretary of State submits annually a comparative report showing all
receipts and disbursements on account of refunds, allowances, and annuities,
together with the total number of persons receiving annuities and the amounts
paid them, and submits also annually estimates of appropriations necessary to
continue the retirement and disability system in fuil force. The law provides that
in no event shall the aggregate total appropriations exceed the aggregate total of
the contributions of the Foreign Service officers theretofore made, and accumulated
interest thereon.-Act of May 24, 1924, Sec. 18 (a).
The Secretary of the Treasury invests from time to time in interest-bearing
securities of the United States such portions of the Foreign Service Retirement
and Disability Fund as in his judgment may not be immediately required for the
payment of annuities, refunds, and allowances, and the income derived from such
investments constitutes a part of said Fund..-Act of May 24, 1924, Sec. 18 (b)
and (g).

37. officers in the Service before July 1, 1924.-Those officers who retire before
having contributed for each year of service shall have withheld from their annu-
ities to the credit of the Foreign Service Retirement and Disability Fund such
proportion of 5 per centum thereof as the number of years in which they did not
contribute bears to the total length of service.-Act of Mtay 24, 1924, Sec. (f).

38. Annuities.-Annuities are paid to retired and disabled Foreign Service
officers wider the following classification, based upon length of service and at the
following percentages of the average annual basic salary for the ten years next
preceding the date of retirement:
Class A, 30 years or more, 60 per centum,
Class B, from 27 to 30 years, 54 per centum.,
Class C, from 24 to 27 years, 48 per centum,
Class D, from 21 to 24 years, 42 per centum,
Class E, from 18 to 21 years, 36 per centum,
Class F, from 15 to 18 years, 30 per centum.
-Act of May 24, 1924, Sec. 18 (e).

39. Employment after retirement.--Whenever any Foreign Service officer, after
the date of his retirement, accepts a position of employment, the emoluments of
which are greater than the annuity received by him from the United States Govern-
ment by virtue of his retirement under the Act of May 24, 1924, the amount of
the said annuity during the continuance of such. employment is reduced by an
equal amount. All retired Foreign Service officers must notify the Secretary of
State once a year of any positions of employment accepted by them stating the
amount of compensation received therefrom and whenever any such officer fails
to so report it is the duty of the Secretary of State to order the payment of the
annuity to be suspended until such report is received.-Act of May 24, 1924, Sec.
18 (in).

40. Separation from the s ervice.-Whenever a Foreign Service officer becomes
separated from the Service except for disability before reaching the age of retire-
ment, 75 per centum of the total amount of contribution from his salary without
interest is returned to him.--Act of May 24, 1924, Sec. 18 (0).

41. Death before retirement.-In case a Foreign Service officer dies without
having reached the retirement age the total amount of his contributions with
accrued interest is paid to his legal representatives.-Act of May 24, 1924, Sec. 18 (i).

42. Death of annuitants.-In case an annuitant dies without having received
in annuities an amount equal 'to the total amount of his contributions from salary
with interest thereon at four per centum per annum compounded annually up
to the time of his death, the excess of the said accumulated contributions over
the said annuity payments is paid to his or her legal representatives.-Act of May
24, 1924, Sec. 18 (i) .

43. Discontinuance of annuity.-When an annuity is discontinued before the
annuitant has received a sum equal to the total amount of his contributions with
accrued interest, the difference is paid to him or to his legal representatives.-Act
of May 24, 1924, Sec. 18 (U).

44. Retirement and disability moneys not subject to legal Process.-None of the
moneys mentioned in Section 18 of the Act of May 24, 1924, are assignable, either
in law or equity, or subject to execution, levy, or attachment, garnishment, or other
legal process.-Act of May 24, 1924, Sec. 18 (h).

45. Recall to Service.-In the event of public emergency any retired Foreign
Service officer may be recalled temporarily to active service by the President and
'while so serving he is entitled in lieu of his retirement allowance to the full pay
of the class in which he is temporarily serving.-Act of May 24, 1924, Sec. Y9.

ARTICLE XXV -,,
COMPENSATION OF CONSULAR OFFICERS

491. Three classes of oficers.-In regard to the sources of their compensation
there are three classes of consular officers, viz., (1) Those who are Foreign Service
officers and receive their compensation as such from appropriations made by
Congress, (2) Those who are not Foreign Service officers but who are paid from
specific appropriations made by Congress, and (3) consular agents receiving no
regular remuneration but who are compensated from the fees collected for official
services and in payments from the Treasury of the United States for services to
American vessels and seamen.

492. Foreign Service o~fficers.-Foreign Service officers assigned to the consular
branch of the Foreign Service receive salaries fixed by law, and are entitled to
compensation at the rate of their respective salaries as Foreign Service officers,
with the following exceptions:

(1) Absence from post. (a) No consular officer shall receive salary for thetime during which he may be absent from his post, by leave or otherwise, beyond
the term of sixty days in the aggregate in any one calendar year; but the timeequal to that usually occupied in going to and from the United States, in case ofthe return, on leave, of such consular officer to the United States may be 'allowed
in addition to the sixty days.--R. S. 174.,2. (b) When a principal officer is absent
i from his post for a period exceeding ten days at any one time, without permission
previously obtained from the President through the Department of State, no
portion of the salary will be allowed for any time in excess of the ten days, unless
the propriety and necessity of the absence shall be made clear to the Department.-
R.8S. 1741;18 Sttt.L. 77.

(2) Recall it1 malfeasance. A consular officer is not entitled to compensation
in case he is recalled for malfeasance, or resigns in anticipation of such recall,
except to the date of such resignation, or of the receipt by him, or at the consulate,of the notification of the recall. In neither case will compensation be allowedt for the time occupied in the transit to the United States.-R. S. 1740; 9 Op. Att.
Gen. 89.

(3) Excess travel time. (a) A consular officer traveling under orders is not
entitled to salary for any time in excess of that actually and necessarily occupiedin performing the journey, by direct route, unless specific orders to the 'cuntrary
have been issued by the Department of State. (b) A consular officer traveling
on leave with permission to visit the United States is not entitled to salary for
H' any time in excess of that actually rzd necessarily occupied in proceeding by
y direct route from his post to the city of Washington and from Washington to hisplace of residence, or .vice versa, unless apeciflc orders to the contrary have been
issued by the Department of State.

493. Compensation when performing diplomatic duties. Within the discretion
of the President, any Foreign Service officer may be appointed to act as commis-sioner, charg6 d'affaires, minister resident, or diplomatic agent for such period as
the public interest may require without loss of grade, class, or salary, provided
that no such officer shall receive more than one salary.-Act of may 04, 1924, Sec.17. With the exception of commissioner, these appointments are subject to con-
firmation by the Senate.

494. Addiional compensation while in charge. For such time as any Foreign
Service officer is lawfully authorized to act as charg6 d'affaires ad interim or to

assume charge of a consulate general or consulate during the a..sence of the prin-
cipal officer at the post to which he shall have been assigned, he receives, if his
salary is less than one-half that of such principal officer, in addition to his salary
as Foreign Service officer, compensation equal to the difference between such
salary and one-half of the salary provided by law for the ambassador, minister or
principal consular officer, as the case may be.-?. S. 1685, as amended, Act of May
24, 19*4, Sec. 17.

allowances out of any money which may have been appropriated for such pur-
pose from time to time by Congress, the expenditure of such representation allow-
ance to be accounted for in detail to the Department of State quarterly under
such rules and regulations as the President may prescribe.-Act of May 24, 1924,

495. Vice consuls not of career.-Vice consuls not of career are compensated as
clerks from the regular clerk hire allowance of the office where their service is
performed. They receive no compensation as vice consuls.
Vice consuls not of career, receiving compensation as clerks, are entitled to
compensation when traveling to and from their posts, or elsewhere, under orders of
the Secretary of State, or while on leavc of absence, subject to the law and regula-
tions governing leaves of absence.
Vice cons.~uls while in charge of a consulate general or consulate during the
absence of the principal officer, are entitled to additional compensation in the same
manner and under the same conditions as Foreign Service officers.-Act of February
27, 19*5.

496. Student interpreters.-Student interpreters receive their salaries as Foreign
Service officers. In addition they may be provided with tuition and quarters.

497. Consular agents.--Consular agents are paid by one-half of the fees received
in their offices, up to a maximum sum of $1,000, in any one year, the other half
being accounted for and paid into the Treasury of the United States. If the total
amount of fees received at a consular agency during a fiscal year exceeds $2,000,
such surplus must be remitted in full to the Treasury of the United States in addi-
tion to the $1,000, due the government as prescribed above.-34 Stat. L. 101.

498. Resignation in the United States.-The right to compensation of a con-
sular officer who resigns while in the United States on leave of absence terminates
with the date of the acceptance of the resignation, or the lapse of his statutory
leave, whichever first occurs.

499. Allowance to widow or heirs:-It has been provided by law that whenever
a consular officer dies in a foreign country in the discharge of his duty, there shall
be paid to his widow, or, if no widow survive him, then to his heirs at law, a sum
of money equal to the allowance made to such officer for the time necessarily occu-
pied in making the transit from his post of duty to his residence in the United
States. The amount is paid directly to the widow, or heirs, as the case may be.-
R. S. Sec. 1749.

500. Compensation provided by law is in full for all servces.-The compensation
allowed by law to the various Foreign Service officers is in full for all the services
rendered and personal expenses incurred by the persons respectively for whom such
compensation is provided, of whatever kind such services or personal expenses may
be, or by whatever treaty, law, or instructions they are required; and no allowance,
other than such as may be specifically provided by law, is made in any case for
the outfit or return home of any such officer or person.-R. S. 174..

501. Fees applicable to salaries.-Foreign Service officers, who are compensated
by salaries appropriated annually by Congress, are authorized to pay themselves
from the fees they may collect as consular otalcers, if these shall be sufficient for the
purpose. If not sufficient, drafts may be drawn. The officer in charge of a con-
sular post is required to pay the salaries of all subordinate officers and employees.
A new paragraph, 220, is established, to read as follows:
.e*o. Consular offers not to have pecuniary interest in wages.-No consular
officer, nor any person under any consular officer shall make any charge or receive,
directly or indirectly, any compensation, by way of commission or otherwise, for
receivir , or disbursing the wages or extra wages to which any seaman or mariner is
entitle,, who is discharged in any foreign country.-R. S. 1719.

14
Paragraph 275 is amended to read as follows:

275. Consular officers not to have pecuniary interest in relief supplies or in hos-
pitals.-No consular officer, nor any person under any consular officer shall make
any charge or receive, directly or indirectly, any compensation, by way of com-
mission or otherwise, for any money advanced to any seaman or mariner who seeks
relief from any consulate; nor be interested, directly or indirectly, in any profit
derived from clothing, boarding or otherwise supplying any such seaman or mani-
ner.-R. S. 1719.
Consular officers are forbidden from owning, maintaining, or having, directly
or indirectly, any pecuniary interest in any hospital abroad to which American
seamen are sent, whether located within or without their respective jurisdictions.
A consular officer known to be so interested, or if interested in like manner in the
supplies furnished to destitute seamen, will be removed. Such cases are within
the prohibition of the statute, and an officer so offending is viable to prosecution
under its provisions.
A new paragraph, 282a, is Established, to read as follows:
282a. Consular officers not to have pecuniary interest in transportation.-No
consular officer, nor any person under any consular officer shall make any charge
or receive, directly or indirectly, any compensation, by way of commission or
otherwise, for sending home any seaman or mariner, but; such prohibition shall not
be construed to relieve or prevent any such officer who is the owner of or otherwise
interested in any vessel of t'" Trnited States, from t. ansportmng in such vessel any
such seaman or mariner, or trom receiving or behiig interested in such reasonable
allowance as may be made for such transportation by law.-R. S. 1719.
Paragraph 440 is amended to read as fol. .vs:
440. Relative rank.-The order of of- precedence in the Service is as follows:
(1) Consuls general; (2) consuls; (3) vice :on..uls who are Foreign Service officers;

(4) student interpreters commissioned as vice consuls; (5) vice consuls who are not
of career; (6) student interpreters not commissioned as vice consuls; (7) consular
agents.
In Paragraph 441 the words "see paragraphs 109, 112" are canceled.
In Paragraph 442 the words "(Paragraph 440) " and "see paragraph 76" are
canceled.
A new Paragraph, numbered 470, is established as follows:

470. Home leave under orders.-The Secretary of State is authorized, whenever
he deems it to be in the public interest, to order to the United States on his statutory
lea-,e of absence any Foreign Service officer who has performed three years or more
of continuous service abroad. The expenses of transportation and subsistence
of such officers and their immediate families, in traveling from their posts to their
homes in the United States and return, are paid under the same rules and regulations
applicable in the case of officers going to and returning from their posts under
orders of the Secretary of State when not on leave. While in the United States
the services of such officers are available for trade conference work or for such
duties in the Department of State as the Secretary of State may prescribe. Act
of May 24, 1925, Sec. 15.
Paragraph 472 is amended to rend as follows :

472. Leave of absence of vice consuls. The regulations in regard to leave of
absence of consular officers are applicable to vice consuls who are of career. Such
officers should apply to the secretary of State for leave, and their applications
Should be transmitted through, and have the approval of, the principal officer
under whom they may be serving. In cases of emergency the principal offic maygrant them conditional leave, reporting the fact to the Secretary of State for
j approval.
A vice consul not of career should make application for leave of absence to his
principal officer when the latter is at his post and in charge of the office and the
principal officer may 'grant leave to the vice consul, reporting the fact to the
Secretary of State.
When a vice consul is in charge of an office he should apply to the Secretary
of State for leave in the same manner as if he were the principal. If there is no
commissioned officer at the post to take charge, the fact should be reported to the

15
Department, by telegraph if necessary, for its consideration. Under no circum-
stances should a consular office, without previous specific authority granted by the
Department, be left in the charge of any person other than a duly commissioned
and bonded American consular officer.
Leave of absence of vice consuls not of career, who receive compensation as
clerks is subject to the limitations governing leave of absence of clerks.
In Paragraph 473, the words " (Paragraph 467) " are canceled.
Paragraphs 476 and 477 are canceled.

CHANGE OF VENUE
The district judge may order a change of venue in any case, civil or criminal,
from one division of said court to the other, whenever in his opinion, in the interest
of justice, such action becomes necessary. Such change of venue may be ordered
upon the motion of the judge, on the application of either party or by consent of

Whenever a change of venue has been ordered by the court, the clerk shall
immediately make out a true transcript of all the orders made in said cause, and
certify thereto under his official see [, and transmit the same with the original papers
in the case to the other division of the district, and the case shall be tried therein
as if it had been instituted there originally.
(Old Rule 2. L. C. Z. 19-197. Ses. 11 & 12, K. . 163)
2
COURT Doc~rs
The clerk, under the advice of the judge and the district attorney, may cause
to be prepared, and shall keep, all such dockets as may be necessary for the pur-
poses of said court.
(OldL Rule3)
3
MoTION DAYS AND DOCKETS
Saturday of each week shall be motion day in the Balboa division of said
court, and the first and third Mondays of each month shall be motion days in the
Cristobal division thereof.
Unless the court is engaged in the trial of a case, such motion days shall be
devoted to hearing motions, demurrers, entering decrees, assigning causes for trial,
confirming reports, entering default judgments, and any other matter ii the con-
duct and preparation of causes preliminary to or after trial.
All motions or other hearings not consented to must be made- in writing, filed
with the clerk, and by him noted upon the book known as the "Motion Docket".
Motions filed in the Balboa division, on or before Thursday of each week shall be
heard on the following Saturday, and motions filed in the Cristobal division on
or before Friday preceding the first and third Mondays of each month shall be
heard on the next following motion day, unless in any case the court orders such

2
hearing deferred; provided that any motion may be heard by consent of the parties
at the conclusion of the regular motion docket, or any motion may be heard at any
time upon the order of the court and upon such notice to the parties as the court
may direct.
(Old Rule 4)
4
PLACING MOTION ON DOCKET is NOTICE.
Any motion or demurrer filed with the clerk and by him placed upon the docket,
shall be notice to opposing counsel, and no further notice need be given except in
those instances where the law requires notice to be otherwise served.
(Old Rule 5)
5
How PLEADINGS AND MOTIONS MAY BE FILED
An answer may be filed in the clerk's office if presented within the time pre-
scribed by the rules or the Code of Civil Procedure. If the time shall have expired
within which an answer or any other pleading must be filed, it may be filed there-
after only by consent of the court. Any pleading which the court directs to be
filed within a given time may be filed in the clerk's office, if presented for filing
within the time prescribed.
Any motion or demurrer may be filed in the clerk's office unless there be some
order of the court or rule of procedure which prohibits the filing thereof, and all
pleadings or motions filed with the clerk must be noted of record by him.
(Old Rule 6)
6
PLEADINGS IN CIVIL ACTIONS
All pleadings and motions in civil cases shall be signed by the attorney or party
to the suit or his duly authorized agent or representative, and shall be endorsed on
the back thereof with the docket number, the name or names of the parties plaintiff
and defendant, the nature of the action, and the name of the attorney of record.
There shall be filed with the original of all motions and all pleadings other than
the complaint, a copy thereof for the adverse party, which shall be endorsed on the
back in like manner as the original; and it shall be the duty of the clerk to show the
date of the filing thereon and promptly deliver or mail such copy to the adverse
party or his attorney of record.
(Old Rule 8)
7
JuR Y
In the trial of any cause, criminal or civil, where a jury trial may be demanded,
if either party shall desire a jury, request theref or must be made at the time when
such cause is assigned for trial. At the trial each side shall be entitled to six per-
emptory challenges. A waiver of a challenge by either party shall preclude such
party, except by consent of court, from thereafter challenging peremptorily any
juror then in the jury box, and the remaining challenges of such party shall be
limited to jurors thereafter called.
(Old Rule 7)
8
EXCEPTIONS
a. An exception is an objection upon a matter of law to a decision made by a
court, tribunal, judge, or other judicial officer, in an action or proceeding. Except
as provided in subsection b. hereof, the exception must be taken at the. time the
decision is made. Rulings of the court upon minor discretionary matters, such as
adjournments, postponements of trials, and the like, shall not be subject to exception.
b. WHAT DEEMED EXCEPTED To: The verdict of the jury, the final decision
it an action or proceeding, an interlocutory order or decision finally determining

8
the rights of the parties or some of them, an order or decision from which an appeal
may be taken, an order sustaining or overruling a demurrer, granting or refusing a
motion to set aside an information, a motion in arrest of judgment, a motion for a
new trial, making or refusing to make an order after. judgment affecting any sub-
stantial rights of the parties, refusing to grant a change of the place of trial, allowing
or refusing to allow an amendment to a pleading, striking out a pleading or a portion
thereof, an order made upon ex parte application, an order or decision made in the
absence of a party, and instructions given or refused, are deemed to have been
excepted to.
(Old Rule 16; Code of Civ. Proc., Sec. 134. Cal. C. C. P., Sec. 646-647. Code of Crim,
Pro., L. C. Z., 206)
9
TIME FOR FILING BILL OF EXCEPTIONS
A bill of exceptions must be prepared, settled, and filed within ten days after
judgment is entered; provided, however, that the court or judge, for good cause
shown, upon application made within such time, may extend the time for preparing,
settling and filing such bill of exceptions, for a period not to exceed sixty days from
the time of making such order; provided, further, that an additional extension of
time beyond that granted by the court may be allowed on stipulation of parties.
(Old Rule 9. Code of Crim. Proc., L. C. Z., 206. Code Civ. Pro., Sec. 136)
10
MOTION FOR NEW TRIAL
A motion for a new trial shall be made only after verdict of the jury or decision
by the court, and before judgment. Such motion shall be filed within five days
after verdict of the jury or decision by the court, unless, for good cause shown,
the court or judge, within such five-day period, extends such time. Such motion
shall be in writing and must set out specifically the grounds upon which the same
is made. When a ground of a motion is the insufficiency of the evidence to justify
the verdict or decision, the motion must specify the particulars in which the evi-
dence is alleged to be insufficient. If a ground of the motion be error in law
occurring at the trial and excepted to by the moving party, the motion must
specify the particular errors upon which the party will rely, and in the case of a
question as to the admissibility of evidence the question, objection or motion,
ruling, and exception thereto must be fully set out. Such motion shall be heard
and determined as speedily as possible after the same is filed.
(Old Rule 10. Cal. C. C. P., Sec. 659)
11
MOTIONS AND ACTIONS TO VACATE OR SET ASIDE JUDGMENTS
A motion to vacate or set aside a judgment or order of the district court must
be in writing, and must be filed within ten days after such judgment or order was
entered except in the case of a default judgment. In the latter case th~e same
must be filed within the time and upon the terms prescribed in Section 106 of the
Code of Civil Procedure, which is hereby re-enacted and adopted by reference as
a part of these rules. Such motion must be accompanied by a showing that a
meritorious defense exists to the cause of action upon which the judgment is based.
Such a motion shall not operate in any case as a stay of execution unless the court
shall so order, or the party applying therefor shall execute a supersedeas bond to
be approved by the court.
An action to reverse, vacate and set aside the judgment of subordinate tribu-
nals, obtained by fraud, accident, mistake or excusable negligence, must be brought
within six months from the rendition of such judgment; otherwise, the procedure
therein as prescribed in Sections 141 to 145, inclusive, of the Code of Civil Proce-
dure, shall be followed, and such sections are hereby re-enacted and adopted by
reference as a part of these rules.
(Old Rule 15. Code Civ. Proc., Sees. 106, 141 to 145)

4
12
ARGUMENTS ON MOTIONS .
No argument of any motion shall be extended beyond thirty minutes to the
side without permission of the court.
(Old Rule 20)
13
TIME FOR MAKING DEFENSE
In all civil actions commenced in the district court, except divorce and
admiralty actions, where personal service has been had, the person served shall
make defense in court within ten days from the service of summons, and where
service by publication is had, within forty days from the last publication of
summons.
(Old Rule 18)
14
TIME WITHIN WicH COURT ORDERS MUST BE PREPARED
When a written order is taken in court, and the attorney for either side is
directed to prepare the order so taken, it shall be prepared and presented to the
court or judge for approval and delivered to the clerk not later than five days
thereafter.-
(Old Rule 19)
15
PREPARING COURT ORDERS
All orders, minutes of proceedings, or actions taken in court, and required to
be made matters of record, must be prepared and recorded not later than one week
from the date when made.
(Old Rule 23)
16
INFORMATIONS
Every offense of which the district court has jurisdiction must be prosecuted
by information signed and verified by the district attorney, or, in the case of his
absence or inability to act, by a~n assistant district attorney appointed by the
Governor of The Panama Canal. The verification must state that the information
is based upon due investigation of the facts relating to the crime charged therein.
All informations so prepared must be filed with the clerk. A criminal cause so
prosecuted shall stand for trial during the term in which the information is filed or
at the next succeeding term, after the apprehension of the defendant, unless for
good cause shown, a continuance thereof to a later date is ordered. Any such
information may be amended in matters of form; bu~t such amended information
must not charge a crime different from the one charged or sought to be charged in
the original information.
(C01i Rule 17. E. 0., p. 97, Code Crim. Pro., Secs., 3, 65, 94, 100. L. C. Z., pp. 173, 183,
187, 188)
17
BONDS TO BE RECORDED
All fiduciary bonds, attachment bonds, bonds required to be executed in all
matters of receivership, injunction proceedings, and any and all other bonds re-
quired by the Code of Civil Procedure, except bonds for cost, bonds for arrest,
or appeal from inferior courts, shall be copied in full and properly indexed by the
clerk in a book kept for that purpose, and such copy, duly authenticated by him,
shall have the force and effect of the original, and the cost of recording shall be
taxed as part of the cost in the court proceeding or action wherein filed, or in the
settlement thereof.
(Old Rule 11)

5U
18
ATTORNEYS ON BOND
Attorneys will not be accepted as sureties upon bonds or Tecognizaflees re-
quired to be filed in court.
(Old Rule 12)
19
BONDS AND COSTS
The Court may at any time before trial require a nonresident plaintiff to file
an undertaking for costs. The defendant may at any time move for security for
costs, and when the motion is made the nonresidence must be shown by affidavit,
unless it is admitted or it appears upon the papers or from the record.
(Old Rule 13)
20
BONDS
In all proceedings in which a bond is required to be given the clerk may accept
a cash deposit in the sum of the bond, a corporate surety, or a personal bond with
approved sureties. No corporate surety may be accepted which is not qualified to
do business in -the Canal Zone. At least one of the sureties on a personal bond
shall be a reieto h.Canal Zone. Where a cash bond is given, money deposited
with the clerk may be withdrawn only upon order of the court.
(Old Rule 14)
21
STENOGRAPHIC NOTES
Whenever, in the discretion of the court, the importance of the case demands,
the judge may cause the testimony in the case, or such part of the testimony as
he may deem proper, to be taken down in shorthand by the official court reporter
connected with the court and qualified to do such work, and the testimony so taken
shall not be transcribed unless so directed by the judge. Provided: Upon approval
of the court, any lawyer practicing before the court may have his own stenographer
in attendance for the purpose of reporting a case for his own personal use.
The original stenographic notes, taken by the court reporter, shall be a part of
the proceedings in the cause; and, unless such notes are filed pursuant to an order
of the judge, directing the stenographer to file the same with the clerk forthwith,
or within a specified time, the same must be carefully preserved by the court reporter
for at least twelve months after the final judgment of the court is rendered. th
Whenever the official court reporter takes down the testimony in a case,th
party making application for such work, except the Government, shall reimburse
to the Government of the Canal Zone the actual time of the court reporter while
thus engaged, no fractional part of a day less than a half day to be calculated;
unless for good and sufficient cause shown the court shall waive this charge.
A party to either a civil or criminal cause, who desires a transcript of the
stenographic notes of the testimony and proceedings therein, or a part thereof,
shall request the court reporter to furnish the same. The court reporter will
furnish to such party an estimate of the cost thereof, and such party, unless it be
the Government, shall deposit with the court reporter the estimated cost of such
transcript, and thereupon the court reporter must furnish such transcript with all
reasonable diligence, to the party requesting the same. The court reporter shall
charge the feesaloe for such service, and shall return to the party making such
deposit any unused portion thereof. The party requesting such transcript shall
be liable for any excess of such fees over such estimate, to be paid before delivery
of such transcript.
(Old Rule 21)

6
29
SUMMONS
The summons issuing from the Court shall read as follows:
UNITED STATES OF AMERICA,
CANAL ZONE
IN THE UNITED STATES DISTRICT COURT OF THE CANAL ZONE
DIVISION OF---------------
Plaintiff.
V.
Defendant.
You are hereby notified to enter your appearance in the office of the clerk of
the above-mentioned court, in writing, and make answer hereto, within ten (10)
days after the service of this summons and copy of the complaint which is hereto
attached, if service be had within the Canal Zone.
And, if served outside of the Canal Zone, you are notified to enter your appear-
ance within forty (40) days after service, and make answer thereto.
Upon the failure to appear within the time aforesaid, the plaintiff will take
judgment against you by default, and demand from the said court the relief applied
for in the complaint.
WITNESS the Honorable------------------ ----------
United States District Judge for the Canal Zone, this-----
day of --------- ,142- .
(Old Rule 22) Cek
23
PROCEDURE ON APPEAL FROM MAGISTRATE'S COURTS
a. In a civil action where an appeal has been perfected from a magistrate's
court to the district court, the party appealing shall pay to the clerk a docket fee
of Five Dollars ($5.00) on or before the first day of the next term of the district
court, or, if the record on appeal is not lodged ten days before the first day of the
next term, then such docket fee shall be paid within ten days after the record on
appeal is lodged with the clerk.. If such docket fee be not paid within the time
fixed, then the appellee may pa$'such fee, and on motion may have the same
judgment entered as that entered in the magistrate's court, plus the appellee's
costs in this court, or a trial of the case in the district court.
b. When such case is docketed the clerk shall notify the parties by mail of
such fact. If not disposed of as provided above by the rendition of judgment,
the plaintiff shall file a written complaint within five days after such notice is mailed,
together with a copy thereof for each defendant. The clerk must then forthwith
mail to each defendant, or his attorney of record, a copy thereof, and the defendant
shall have five days after such mailing to plead thereto. Where the defendant
files a cross complaint the same procedure shall be followed as provided above

7
upon the filing of the plaintiff's complaint. Such time for filing pleadings may be
extended by the court or judge. In framing the issues and in the trial and deter-
mination of such action on the merits, except as provided herein, the same procedure
shall be followed as in a case originally commenced in the district court.
c. Such action shall be tried and determined in the district court on the same
issues presented in the magistrate's court; provided, however, that where an appeal
is taken from a default judgment, the party defaulted may, upon timely application
to the district court and upon a clear showing of mistake, surprise, inadvertence,
or excusable neglect, be admitted to plead upon such terms as may be imposed.
No pleading or amendment thereto shall be allowed which will increase the recovery
beyond the jurisdiction of the magistrate's court. The issues in the magistrate's
court shall be determined from the record on appeal transmitted by the magistrate
to the clerk of this court.
(New and Code Civ. Pro., Sec. 68-10.5)
d. In criminal actions appealed from a magistrate's court, the affidavit may
be amended in this court as to matters of form or substance where the rights of
the defendant are not substantially prejudiced thereby; but the amended affidavit
may not charge a crime different from that charged, or sought to be charged, in
the original affidavit.
e. If it shall appear from the record on appeal or otherwise be made clearly
to appear to the satisfaction of the district court, that the transcript of a magis-
trate's court does not show all of the proceedings in said court required by law to
be shown therein, unless such defects be waived, the following proceedings may
be had : The district court shall forthwith notify the magistrate in writing of. the
precise matter to be considered and allow him to amend his return according to
the facts. If he neglects or refuses so to do, the district court may issue a rule
requiring such magistrate to appear and show cause why his return should not be
amended; but he shall, in no case, be required to amend his return unless it shall
clearly appear that the return does not show the proceedings according to the
facts.
(Code Civ. Pro., Sec. 71)
24
LIBERAL CONSTRUCTION-AUTHORITY OF JUDGE
The foregoing rules shall be construed to promote justice. Where the Codes
of Criminal or Civil Procedure or these rules fail to specify a procedure in any given
case or matter, the court or the judge may adopt and follow such procedure as will
insure the due administration of justice between the parties.
(New)
CALVIN COOLIDGE
THE WrITE HOUSE,
July 28, 1925.

Military Reservation known as Camp Sherman, together with all improvements

sions of the Act of Congress approved August 9, 1921, (42 Stat. 147-150), excepting:
